title: Renner's 2027 NFL Draft scouting series: Ranking the top 10 offensive tackles
summary: Trevor Goosby enters as the clear OT1, but Jordan Seaton, Lance Heard and several high-upside athletes could push for Round 1 status
full_text:
This class has a little bit of everything. It's got a couple of All-World athletes that would be top-10 picks already if we held the draft tomorrow. It's got a trio of inexperienced tackles who are a tier below physically, but showed high-end coordination in their limited action. It's got two prodigiously powerful tackles who throw around SEC defensive ends. And it's got a couple of incredibly nimble offensive tackles with play strength concerns. By the time next spring rolls around, I would guess we'll see another half-dozen or so tackles end up going amongst the top-32.
Positional rankings: IOL • S • LB • DT • TE • OT • RB • CB • EDGE • WR • QB
Note: ⭐️ represents each player's 247Sports star rating as a high school recruit
Trevor Goosby would have been my top tackle if he had come out after last season, but with only a year and a half of starting experience, Goosby opted to return to a loaded Texas roster. Physically, there are no holes to poke in his game. He's got an ideal frame, ideal size, ideal movement skills and ideal ability to generate power. While he started slowly in 2025, by the end of the season, his tape was dominant. If we see that same guy or even a better one in 2026, Goosby will quite comfortably be the best senior offensive tackle prospect this decade.
Trevor Goosby pic.twitter.com/QZROmOvpfk
Jordan Seaton is the kind of "know it when you see it" athlete for the position who has everything you could want to hang with NFL-caliber athletes on the edge. Quick feet, long arms, and urgent hands are his calling cards. I'm not too worried about those translating to a bump up in competition in the SEC after playing last year at Colorado.
I am still worried about the run game, where Seaton isn't much of a people mover and can struggle to sustain blocks. He reminds me a bit of Olu Fashanu because of that. With a good season, he'll likely be drafted higher than Fashanu's 11th-overall selection.
Jordan Seaton pass pro pic.twitter.com/tvCBvcM0vn
I couldn't help but be reminded, when watching Lance Heard 's tape last year at Tennessee, of a recent first-round tackle by the Volunteers. Herald prodigious power in his hands that's reminiscent of Darnell Wright's senior tape. What separates those two from a lot of strong offensive tackles is how much they relish hitting defenders. You see it especially on the move, where Heard will lay his body on the line as a puller.
New Kentucky OT Lance Heard is one of the most violent pullers I've ever seen pic.twitter.com/Nso7UX6YHy
I may be getting out over my skis a little for a player with 150 career snaps who hasn't even been named a starter yet this fall, but that's how confident I feel about Ian Moore 's projectable traits. Specifically, his understanding of blocking angles and how to recover. You saw it all over his 31 snaps against the likes of Rueben Bain Jr. and Akheem Mesidor for Miami in the playoffs last year. I'm not going to act like he won the matchups, but he held his own for a true sophomore and fought to stay in contact for reps he lost.
If Ian Moore can win the starting left tackle job for Ohio State it allows Austin Siereveld to move back to guard. I think that gives the Buckeyes their best offensive line. pic.twitter.com/13ZpeMiP5k
I don't love that he's headed to his third SEC school in four years this fall, and I think his technical development has been stunted because of that. The ceiling is so sky-high, though, if he were to ever really put it all together.
Trevor Lauck was another first-year starter in 2025 who was so proficient on tape already that he could have left school early. He made the right decision to return to Iowa, though, as their developmental pipeline is as good as it gets in college football . He's got some of the best hands in this tackle class, not only with their placement, but also with their ability to stay latched. While Iowa's offense doesn't leave its tackles on islands much in pass protection, Lauck showed easy agility to mirror speed when asked to do so. His issues arose more with letting defenders into his chest and getting walked back into the pocket. If his overall play strength improves this year, he has a good shot to go round 1.
Trevor Lauck (#59) Iowa ✅ Allowed just 6 pressures all season in 2025 on over 700 snaps ✅ Quick off the snap ✅ Recognizing and passing off stunts and games at the line ✅ Adept at sealing off defenders ✅ 87.8 pass block grade in 2025 ✅ 79.7 run block grade during 2025 pic.twitter.com/395yFMvtmV
Niki Prongos may be on the older side for a tackle as a fifth-year senior (only two of the 37 first-round offensive tackles this decade have been fifth- or sixth-year prospects), but when you consider that he only started playing football his senior year of high school, it changes that equation a little. While you saw that greenness on tape in his first year as a starter in 2025, you also saw incredible natural talent. I love his body control and how he brings a stable base with him everywhere he goes. Athletes who move as he does at 6-foot-7, 312 pounds tend to figure it out. And it was clear on tape as the season progressed that he was already finding more answers with more reps.
Love to see Stanford LT Niki Prongos (6-7, 315) 🌲Didn't play 🏈 until senior year of HS 🌲Played RG/RT 3 years at UCLA May be “raw” in experience, but his athleticism off the ball, engagement, & in space understanding leverage & recovery➡️early “My Guy” pic.twitter.com/IIkFNOahnL
There are two main reasons I think Cayden Green is better suited to guard than to play on the exterior, despite having the frame to play either. The first is his modest foot speed, which can get him in trouble against better athletes. The second is his ease in handling power moves. He absorbs contact extremely well and delivers it about as well, too. I was very impressed with how consistently he sinks his hips into contact in the run game to win leverage battles. I found myself appreciating his tape the more I watched, and I'm guessing NFL teams will, too. There's a good chance he's the first guard off the board in April.
Cayden Green (Missouri) is my #1 guard in the 2026 class. 320 lb mauler entering his true JR year, but already has 1.5 years of starting experience. Strong anchor, precise hands, & consistently gets movement at the POA. pic.twitter.com/jEPlBuCAxH
Jacarrius Peak was the most difficult player for me to rank in the tackle class. He is, without a doubt, the most impressive mover in this tackle class. He could legitimately pass for a tight end and should even test like one next spring. On the flip side, he has a tiny frame for an offensive tackle. It's not only that he's light at 6-foot-4, 292 pounds, but also that he's thin in the upper body. On tape, he handles speed-rushers with ease, but power-rushers can walk him back routinely. While he found more answers with his hands re-leveraging last year to mitigate that concern, there's only so much you can do without the heft. If his weight and play strength can improve this season, he could easily be a first-rounder.
Jacarrius Peak (#65) South Carolina ✅ Feldman Freak List that can reportedly run a 4.8 40-yard dash ✅ Quick to engage defenders out of his stance ✅ Mirroring ability in pass pro. ✅ Over 2,200 career snaps played entering the 2026 season ✅ 84.1 pass block grade in 2025 pic.twitter.com/lveNz7vl9F
Elijah Paige missed six games last year and went out early from a couple of others in an injury-plagued redshirt sophomore campaign. He got his first start in the Holiday Bowl as a true freshman in 2023 and has been the starting left tackle for USC ever since. He's got an obvious NFL tackle frame with easy movement skills to boot. I love his ability to mirror speed while staying in control and on balance. His hands have to improve in pass protection to protect himself from bull rushes, which he struggled to sit down on at 6-foot-7. He has the experience and physical tools; now he just needs to stay healthy for a full…

title: Winning a Super Bowl isn't enough for Ben Johnson: Here's what Bears coach wants to accomplish in 2026
summary: Of course, Johnson wants to win the Super Bowl, but he also wants to do it in a dominant fashion
full_text:
Expectations are fairly high for the Chicago Bears entering the 2026 season. They're coming off a year where they went 11-6 under first-year head coach Ben Johnson, then won a playoff game against the division rival Green Bay Packers before losing in overtime to the Los Angeles Rams in the divisional round. They have an ascending quarterback in Caleb Williams and an exciting group of skill-position talent led by players like Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III . They figure to be one of the most exciting teams to watch this year.
And if Johnson has his way, that'll certainly be the case. Because Johnson has a goal beyond just doing better than the team did last season, and even beyond winning the Super Bowl -- which is certainly a surprise, given that pretty much everyone in the league agrees on that being their ultimate goal in any given season.
"You've got 31 other teams coming to training camp saying, 'Our goal is to win the Super Bowl,'" Johnson said, via The Athletic . "I want more than that. I want to have the highest-scoring offense ever, which happens to be the 2013 Denver Broncos . I know how many points per game they scored (37.9), and I want to surpass them. I want shutouts. I want blowouts."
The 2013 Broncos indeed hold the points-per-game record, having scored more than a full point per game more than the next-closest team (the 2007 Patriots ). Here's a look at the rest of the top 10 in points-per-game during the Super Bowl era:
The Bears were at 25.9 points per game last year, a figure that ranked ninth in the NFL . That means they'll have to jump by more than 12 points per game in order to surpass the 2013 Broncos.
The current record for points-per-game increase from one season to the next is held by the 2017 Rams, who jumped from 14.0 points per game in one season to 29.9 in the next. That's an increase of 15.9 points per game. There are only nine other teams that made a jump of at least 12 points per game from one season to the next: the 1999 Rams, 1975 Colts , 2013 Chiefs, 2010 Raiders , 2011 Panthers , 2007 Patriots, 1983 Washington, 1998 Vikings and 2016 Falcons.
The thing about the Bears is, they might need to show great improvement offensively in order to meet the expectations they've set for themselves this year, because their defense is dealing with a ton of injury issues at the moment, particularly in the secondary.
Free agent acquisition Coby Bryant will miss four-to-six months after knee surgery. Kyler Gordon is without a timetable to return to the field. Even guys like Cam Lewis and Tyrique Stevenson either left or missed recent practices. This was a defense that was counting on Bryant's arrival and Gordon's return from injury to do a lot of the heavy lifting in terms of making improvements this year, and it doesn't look like it's going to get either of those things.
Therefore, it might be up to the offense to help stave off any regression the Bears might be due for after they won so many one-score games last season, which generally doesn't hold up year over year. Johnson acknowledged earlier this offseason that the Bears are the league's No. 1 regression candidate, but he has goals even beyond bucking the regression trends. He wants to set the record for most consecutive wins, as well.
"Why can't we do that?" Johnson said, again via The Athletic. "There has never been an undefeated season (since teams have been playing more than 14 regular-season games). The moon is the Super Bowl, but we're shooting beyond that, for the stars. And I want these players to feel that each and every single day they come in."
Johnson certainly isn't afraid of setting lofty goals for his team. Whether they can achieve those goals is an open question.
author: Jared Dubin

title: Training camp overreactions: Kyler Murray's ups and downs concerning? Laremy Tunsil injury dooms Commanders?
summary: With the first week of the preseason here, some headlines are important, while others aren't
full_text:
When training camps begin, everything is hunky-dory. The grass is green. The players are back and in the best shape of their lives. The new systems are going to help said players reach new heights. No one has lost a game.
And then, as the weeks go on, the bumps and bruises appear. Maybe not every player is going to take that next step. (Duh.) Maybe some even take a step back. Maybe the best-case-scenario outcomes that seemed so likely in late July are looking less and less likely. Every coach wants competition -- for starting spots, for playing time, for roster spots -- but what if those competitions simply aren't up to snuff?
This is the NFL , where a strength one day can be a weakness the next, where hope one day can be worry the next. The rose-colored glasses come off quickly.
The best teams are the ones with the best combinations of talent, depth, luck and coaching, of course, but they're also the ones that can make accurate, level-headed assessments and decisions as the regular season approaches rapidly. What matters and what doesn't in these crucial weeks?
It's important to be urgent but not antsy, and that goes not just for front offices, coaches and players, but for those evaluating all of them as well. As such, we're determining whether some notable training camp storylines are overreactions -- from minor to significant to major -- or not.
The Vikings made official Tuesday what had long been expected: Kyler Murray is the Week 1 starter against the Packers . The path to getting there, though, wasn't the most inspiring. Murray basically beat out J.J. McCarthy by default.
It seemed like McCarthy made up ground over the weekend, per Bring Me The Sports' Will Ragatz , when ESPN's Kevin Seifert said Murray had "hit a wall" . In a way one could view this as Murray simply retaining his position as the favorite long enough for Kevin O'Connell to make a decision.
It's easy to look at Murray's up-and-down training camp -- coming off a strange, underwhelming, injured finish to his time with the Cardinals -- and think the Vikings are in quarterback purgatory again. But that'd be wrong. Last year, the Vikings were among the worst-quarterbacked teams in the NFL. Murray at his very worst has been roughly average.
Murray at his worst is significantly better than what the Vikings produced last year, and one could argue he now has the best supporting cast of his career.
During minicamp, Murray said splitting reps was making his transition to a new team more difficult . If he was always going to be the starter, it makes sense to give him every advantage possible by declaring him the starter even before a preseason game . In fact, Murray had one of his best practices Tuesday, hours after being named starter.
Maybe Murray isn't a great quarterback, or even a good one. But if he can be average, the Vikings, who went 9-8 last year despite awful quarterback play, could get back to the postseason.
The first big headline to come out of Patriots training camp was A.J. Brown dropping a pass and Mike Vrabel ripping into him . The next big headline was how few headlines Brown was producing. It was a slow start for Brown, and going against elite cornerback Christian Gonzalez certainly contributed. The two have been jawing back and forth, and it escalated during one practice last week .
Worrying about that, though, is a classic training camp overreaction, and a short-sighted one at that. Brown looked good in this week's joint practice with the Colts , beating Sauce Gardner on one route ...
A.J. Brown just DUSTED Sauce Gardner in 1v1s🔥 Patriots fans in attendance LOVE IT - @CLNSMedia pic.twitter.com/0g1GBXTSjf
... and scoring a touchdown on a seven-on-seven rep.
Maye to AJB for 6 pic.twitter.com/f6Ezt7R8Bu
Brown fits Drake Maye's game perfectly , but he admitted it was an adjustment.
"It started off a little slow," Brown said , per ESPN. "Obviously because I'm going against Gonzo and [Maye] is getting to know me more and more. But as these practices have been going, me and him have been picking up very good momentum."
Let's put this one to bed quickly. Cousins may no longer be a upper-middle or even middle-tier starter, but he can still play. And he should play Week 1 over Fernando Mendoza . Take it from ESPN's Ryan McFadden :
"He has played solely with the starters, as expected, and has looked better than Mendoza and Aidan O'Connell . Cousins has been efficient and has rarely put the ball in harm's way. On top of that, the players have brought Cousins in as one of the leaders on the team."
Plus, Tom Brady doesn't like rookie quarterbacks playing right away , either.
It behooves Mendoza to sit at least a few weeks, to learn the ins and outs of weekly game prep, to learn what Cousins sees in-game, to not be thrown into the fire too early. Mendoza won't succeed (or fail) because he got his first start in Week 5 rather than in Week 1.
I see a lot of social media posts during training camp because, as I've noted, training camp is a time for reactions -- measured reactions and overreactions alike. Some names pop up more than others, and I don't think anyone has popped up more often in a more positive way than Parker Washington . It seems like he's doing cool stuff all the time.
Every day is Parker day 😮‍💨 @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/GnCwKM30Yd
Notes and unofficial stats from the Jaguars' Teal & White mock game (Teal won 19-12): QB Trevor Lawrence was 15 of 29 passes for 212 yards and 3 TDs. Parker Washington, Brian Thomas Jr., and LeQuint Allen had TD catches. Washington had six catches for 118 yards and TD.
That's because Washington is a really cool player and, more importantly, a really good player. Last year, he led the NFL in contested catch rate, per Pro Football Focus , despite standing 5-10. Over his last four games (including postseason), he had 26 catches for 454 yards and three touchdowns.
For all the good news surrounding Brian Thomas Jr . and all the good things Jakobi Meyers did for the offense last year and all the talent Travis Hunter has, Washington is in line for a major breakout campaign. He quietly led Jacksonville in receiving yards last year and will loudly repeat that this year.
The biggest headline the Browns and the Cardinals made this offseason was moving on from players who were thought to be franchise pillars. Cleveland sent Myles Garrett to the Rams , and Arizona split with Murray.
Neither team is expected to be very good this season, either. But that doesn't mean things are completely lost.
For Cleveland, wide receivers Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion have impressed big time. Boston has been busiest wide receiver by far , and his combination of huge size and smooth moving is impressive.
Denzel Boston Is Looking Like the NFL’s BEST Rookie WR in Training Camp So Far...😳 pic.twitter.com/s4qa5SwUlj
But Concepcion has impressed , too. He's more of a jittery slot receiver -- Todd Monken had Zay Flowers in Baltimore, and that would be the high-end comparison here.
The Browns also have rookie left tackle Spencer Fano already inserted as a starter. Add in Quinshon Judkins and Harold Fannin Jr. , both in their second year, and you see a solid young core forming. On defense, Jared Verse , acquired in the Garrett trade, and Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger are the bright young spots, and stud corner Denzel Ward just got an extension, too. Cleveland has a lot going right and a ton of trade capital in the future.
The Cardinals already had Trey McBride , Marvin Harrison Jr . and Michael Wilson at the pass-catching spots, but adding Jeremiyah Love third overall adds some score-from-anywhere juice, too.
#Cardinals Jeremiyah Love is going to be special. Seamlessly hits all the gaps, deep make a man miss bag, and isn’t afraid of contact. He may be Gibbs and Bijan combined pic.twitter.com/l93QSkzAS7
Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr . is excellent when healthy, and second-round pick Chase Bisontis should start right away at guard. Heck, even…
author: Zachary Pereles

title: NFL preseason rookie watch list: Cowboys LB, Denzel Boston headline top 10 to monitor
summary: Beyond the first-round draft picks, these under-the-radar rookies are already turning heads in training camp
full_text:
The Hall of Fame game was a delicious hors d'oeuvres for the remainder of the NFL preseason . The league's other teams join in the excitement, beginning today and continuing through the end of the month. For many, preseason games are the first impressions fans have of rookies. Who are some of those rookies who deserve significant attention?
Having already analyzed several rookies in different formats (noteworthy Pro Football Hall of Fame game participants and rookies competing for starting roles ), the intention was to bring new names to the table. The first-round picks were also excluded because that is low-hanging fruit; specifically, the top half of the round. For example, it goes without saying that everyone wants to see Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza , who will be sidelined for part of the regular season.
Here are 10 rookies to monitor through the preseason:
Allen has been the talk of Chiefs camp, drowning out concerns of the team declining to add more help for Patrick Mahomes . Although he is playing for his fourth team in as many seasons, the fifth-round pick has the top-end speed and suddenness to be a big-play threat in Kansas City. They need more consistency from a unit that has failed to provide it for a variety of reasons. Xavier Worthy and Rashee Rice are the only returning receivers with at least 20 receptions last season.
Barham is a good fit in Christian Parker's defensive scheme because he has the versatility to play more of an off-ball role and fit run gaps or overload the line of scrimmage as an extra rusher. Philadelphia has had players like Jihaad Campbell , Zack Baun and Nolan Smith to execute the Vic Fangio scheme. Barham's background has a similar flavor.
Bernard's participation is like a science experiment. He has never played football, but has off-the-charts athletic potential within his 6-foot-4-inch frame. The Eagles bought a lottery ticket in the seventh round and hope it turns into another Jordan Mailata . Mailata is the exception, however, and not the rule.
Philadelphia also has edge rusher Joshua Weru , who is coming through the International Player Pathway Program.
Will the on-field production match the training camp hype? Few rookies have generated as much buzz as Boston to this point. The problem is that the public may not be able to make an accurate assessment of the player's ability to catch passes from that quarterback collective in northeast Ohio.
Boston has already been named the starting X receiver. The team likes that the second-round pick is also an asset in the run game. First-round pick KC Concepcion will likely be moved around and put in motion the way Zay Flowers had been in Baltimore with Todd Monken.
There has been a palpable buzz regarding Demmings, a fifth-round pick out of Stephen F. Austin. His former teammate, cornerback Jalen Mayo, will have an opportunity to be drafted next year after transferring to Houston.
Cornerback has been an evergreen position of need for the Vikings . They signed Isaiah Rodgers and James Pierre each of the past two offseasons, but Demmings could be a viable long-term option for the franchise if he pans out.
Golday may be listed as a linebacker, but his strength last season was rushing the passer. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores' scheme is ultra-aggressive, so Golday's versatility, especially at 6-foot-4 and 240 pounds, makes him an asset. He has generated a lot of positive feedback in training camp and is still just two years removed from Central Arkansas.
How big of a role will he earn Week 1?
Lane is another rookie receiver drawing rave reviews from camp. The coaching staff is different, but Baltimore has been searching for a taller receiver for years. They had done the DeAndre Hopkins experiment, but double-dipped in this year's draft with Elijah Sarratt and Lane. The hope is that Lane can allow them to play above the rim, but also spring Derrick Henry in the run game.
After Thursday night of the 2026 NFL Draft , I spoke on CBS Sports HQ about how McDonald would be a great fit for DeMeco Ryans ' team if he lasted until Houston's second-round pick. The Texans have been able to squeeze every ounce of juice from well-traveled veteran oranges early in Ryans' tenure, but McDonald brings a reliability they have not yet possessed.
Despite pushing 330 pounds, McDonald has a bit more explosion than one would expect from an interior run stuffer, which will force difficult decisions from opposing teams tasked with blocking Will Anderson Jr. , Danielle Hunter and McDonald.
Although listed second team on the depth chart, Perkins is already earning repetitions with the first team in training camp. Again, in the modern NFL , there are expanded opportunities for hybrid linebackers capable of rushing the passer, as well as down-to-down responsibilities. Perkins had fulfilled both linebacker and edge rusher roles early in his time at LSU; that had been viewed as a negative, but it may prove to be a blessing in disguise in the right scheme.
Fellow rookie Kendal Daniels is pushing for playing time in competition with Christian Harris and Divine Deablo as well.
Tampa Bay had to replace Devin White , then they had to replace veteran Lavonte David ; the latter is not an assignment for the faint of heart. Fortunately, second-round pick Josiah Trotter -- the son of NFL legend Jeremiah Trotter -- has been a revelation early in camp. It sounds as though he is the leader in the clubhouse for the starting job next to veteran Alex Anzalone .

title: NFL preseason 2026: Eight teams that need August reps the most, from Dolphins to Browns
summary: From high-stakes quarterback battles in Cleveland to massive roster overhauls in Miami, eight teams have the most at stake this NFL preseason
full_text:
The NFL preseason is upon us, and this is where roster spots are solidified. Depth charts form and position battles are settled. All 32 coaching staffs use these exhibition matchups to figure out who fits their systems best and to unearth gems that went overlooked during the draft. Whether fans care or not, the preseason is important, and it's important for some teams more than others. There are first-year head coaches getting their feet wet, new quarterbacks in new situations and massive questions that need answering before things kick off for real in September.
Below, we will break down eight NFL teams that need this preseason the most for one reason or another.
New QB : The Miami Dolphins don't have a quarterback battle, but they do have a new signal-caller. Malik Willis flashed starting potential in limited action with the Green Bay Packers over the last two years, but it was a pretty small sample size. However, he proved he could run Matt LaFleur's system. Now, Willis is learning a new Bobby Slowik system and does not have the kind of weaponry he benefited from in Green Bay. These preseason reps are essential.
WR battle : Speaking of weaponry, who will be Willis' primary receivers with Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle gone? That remains to be seen. Malik Washington is the returning leader, but Miami also brought in Jalen Tolbert and TuTu Atwell in free agency. Then, there are the rookies. In the third round, the Dolphins drafted the 6-foot-4 Caleb Douglas and then Chris Bell out of Louisville, who is coming off a torn ACL. Two rounds later, Miami landed Kevin Coleman Jr . out of Missouri, who was a productive slot weapon. So which one of these players is going to stand out the most?
Chance to look at the secondary: The Dolphins' secondary has some question marks and appears to be one of the worst in the NFL on paper. To make matters worse, several players on the back end are banged up right now as well.
New general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan spent the No. 27 overall pick on former San Diego State corner Chris Johnson , who figures to start immediately. He was named the 2025 Mountain West Co-Defensive Player of the Year after allowing the lowest passer rating (10.9) in the FBS last season. That cornerback room also includes Jason Marshall Jr., Darrell Baker Jr. , Storm Duck , Marco Wilson and JuJu Brents. Believe it or not, Marshall and Wilson are the only ones healthy right now.
At safety, Dante Trader Jr. , Zayne Anderson , Lonnie Johnson Jr. and Louis Moore are competing for spots. Also, keep an eye on fifth-round pick Michael Taaffe out of Texas. This was a First Team All-SEC player who could surprise some people despite his size. A lot to be sorted out in Miami's secondary.
QB battle : It's obvious. Instead of relying on Cleveland Browns reporters and social media, we finally get to see how this quarterback battle is shaping up for ourselves. I'm guessing Deshaun Watson probably has the inside track for the job, but at the same time, I don't have to tell you that he's been terrible ever since being dealt from Houston. Shedeur Sanders wasn't great as a rookie, but he did inject some hope into the franchise. It's clear his internal clock is slow, and that's something that has to change if he's going to be a legitimate starter in this league. I'm not going to change my initial prediction that Watson will win this battle, but I'd love to see Sanders make it a tough call for Todd Monken.
Remade offensive line : Did you know the Browns are the only team since 1970 to lose its top five offensive line starters all in the same offseason? Granted, this unit wasn't good in 2025 and was hit hard by injuries, but it's true. Cam Robinson , Joel Bitonio , Ethan Pocic , Wyatt Teller and Jack Conklin are gone. This year, first-round pick Spencer Fano is expected to start at left tackle, Zion Johnson at left guard, Elgton Jenkins at center, Teven Jenkins at right guard and then the versatile Tytus Howard at right tackle. All of these players are brand new to each other, so some live reps in the preseason will serve them well as a collective unit.
WR rotation : I've already written about why the Browns' wide receiving corps is one of the most interesting position battles in the NFL this season. Jerry Jeudy is the veteran in the room, but with his dropsies, he's no Justin Jefferson . No. 24 overall pick KC Concepcion was a First Team All-SEC player thrice over the last year as a Swiss Army Knife, then there's the big-bodied Denzel Boston out of Washington. He's 6-foot-4 and possesses these strong hands that make him an attractive target. Don't overlook Isaiah Bond either. He went undrafted out of Texas last year due to off-field issues, but possesses legitimate speed and is a weapon after the catch.
New coach and new roster : Not only do the Las Vegas Raiders have a new first-year coach in Klint Kubiak, but they also have maybe one of the most-improved rosters on paper. I mean that -- especially on the defensive side of the ball. Maxx Crosby has a new running mate in Kwity Paye , there are two new starting off-ball linebackers in Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker , and a new nickel in the veteran Taron Johnson . One of their rookies should play an important role as well. The Raiders drafted Arizona defensive back Treydan Stukes at No. 38 overall and paired him with teammate Dalton Johnson in the fifth. Vegas also grabbed a potential steal in Tennessee corner Jermod McCoy at No. 101 overall. A lot of new players in Sin City.
Fernando Mendoza : If the Raiders won't give Mendoza immediate regular-season reps, he has to get them in the preseason. Sure, a young quarterback can benefit by sitting and learning behind a veteran like Kirk Cousins , but live game reps are where a player learns the most. This will be his only chance to experience those live reps before he's thrown into the starting lineup at some point this season.
Wide receivers : I thought the Raiders had maybe the worst wide receiving corps in the NFL last season, and all they did this offseason was add Jalen Nailor and draft Malik Benson in the sixth round. Tre Tucker was their leading receiver last year with 696 yards and five touchdowns, and more is expected of second-year pass-catchers Jack Bech and Dont'e Thornton Jr . We know Brock Bowers will likely be Cousins' top target, but the wide receivers are important, too. Which one of these young players will step up?
Key position battles : Aaron Glenn told reporters that everybody will play in the New York Jets ' preseason opener, and I love that. Because the Jets have a few key position battles to sort out. Azareye'h Thomas and Pro Bowler Nahshon Wright are fighting for the right to start opposite Brandon Stephens , while Andre Cisco , Dane Belton and Malachi Moore are battling to start next to Minkah Fitzpatrick at safety. Then there's the nickel spot, which Jarvis Brownlee Jr . will look to lock down with rookie D'Angelo Ponds sidelined due to a calf strain.
Speaking of rookies, some first-year players are battling for playing time.
High expectations for first-year players : When the Jets' initial depth chart dropped, they did not list any rookies as starters. No. 2 overall pick David Bailey is a backup pass rusher to Kingsley Enagbare , the injured No. 16 overall pick Kenyon Sadiq is slated to back up Mason Taylor at tight end, while No. 30 overall pick Omar Cooper Jr . is listed behind Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell . The preseason will be Bailey's and Cooper's first NFL action. If they impress, they will move up the depth chart quicker. It goes without being said that fans have very high hopes for these rookies. These preseason reps are important.
QB battle : The Atlanta Falcons are hosting somewhat of a quarterback battle with Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr . Tagovailoa is the frontrunner since Penix hasn't been cleared for 11-on-11 work due to his torn ACL, and it's unknown if he will even be able to play in the preseason. Still, this is an…

It may seem a bit pedantic, it is the preseason, but for a team that is the most losingest in North American Sports history, winning is not something to take lightly. So, for the Arizona Cardinals, to get a 27-14 victory on the road against the Las Vegas Raiders, forgive us for enjoying it. It started with Jacoby Brissett and the starters answering the Raiders opening drive touchdown with one of their own, knotting things up at 7-7. Brissett was a cool 5/5 for 44 yards and a touchdown, before he gave way to Gardner Minshew who was 14/16 for 101 yards and two touchdowns. We also saw Jeremiyah Love’s Cardinals debut, where he had 11 carries for 58 yards and three receptions for 14 yards in an impressive, if not a bit much of a performance with 14 touches in the preseason. It was another great effort from the Cardinals offense and a better effort from their defense, although the Raiders top two quarterbacks were 15/22 for 147 yards and two touchdowns. Also, we have to ask, does the quarterback play make last weeks effort by Carson Beck (who was out with a rib injury) a little less impressive? The biggest takeaway from the game though is that rookie second round pick Chase Bisontis left the game with an apparent knee injury.

title: What to know about Falcons – Broncos preseason Week 1
summary: The Falcons! The Broncos! Backups! Deep reserves! It’s all here in Week 1 of preseason. Here’s everything you need to know about tomorrow night’s game, which is likely to be sloppy football but fun nonetheless, not to mention important given all the roster battles that are going on. Let’s dive in. Roster battles to monitor […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 17: Quarterback Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons calls a play at the line of scrimmage during the second half of an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on November 17, 2024 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Falcons! The Broncos! Backups! Deep reserves! It’s all here in Week 1 of preseason. Here’s everything you need to know about tomorrow night’s game, which is likely to be sloppy football but fun nonetheless, not to mention important given all the roster battles that are going on. Let’s dive in. Roster battles to monitor QB3 Cooper Rush will be first up in Friday’s game and is the veteran, so he’ll have a real leg up on this competition. Jack Strand, meanwhile, has been far better than an undrafted free agent quarterback usually is and will have a chance to make his case in a real game. RB3 New arrival Trey Sermon can push Nate Carter, Tyler Goodson, and to a lesser extent Cash Jones for a role. I think Jones will latch on to a practice squad spot owing to his receiving ability and special teams prowess, so the real competition figures to be Sermon versus Carter versus Goodson. A quality first preseason game could give one of them a major boost, especially Sermon as a new face. WR5/6 As always, there are many competitors here and not a lot of room on the roster. Chris Blair has been here a long time and is having another fine summer, while rookie UDFA Vinny Anthony is rolling. Antwane Wells Jr., Keelan Marion, Kristian Wilkerson, and Dylan Drummond round out the competition, and as is always the case, one of these guys will get hot in preseason and push for a role. C2 Corey Levin and James Brockermeyer are duking it out, and this one’s fun because Levin brings a connection to Bill Callahan and long experience in the league and Brockermeyer is an intriguing undrafted free agent with no experience but plenty of talent. Levin promises reliability, but Brockermeyer’s upside makes him a player well worth watching. ILB2 Maybe the most compelling battle of them all. Christian Harris, Kendal Daniels, and Harold Perkins Jr. are all competing for a starting job next to Divine Deablo, and they’ve all had their turns working as starters in training camp. With Deablo already a little banged up, the pecking order could matter a great deal here, and we’ll be watching all three closely to see how good they look in live game action. CB2/3 There’s some legitimately interesting subplots here, too. Is Mike Hughes ticketed for #2 duties again, or can Avieon Terrell take that over? Will Billy Bowman Jr. be healthy enough to seize the nickel job, or are Terrell and Darnay Holmes leading the way for that competition? Performance and when we see these players out there on Friday night will give us some early clues. What’s new with the Broncos? The Broncos didn’t overhaul their roster after making the playoffs in 2026 with a young quarterback and core and odious headset-wearing orc Sean Payton still roaming the sidelines, but they saw an opportunity to go further in the postseason and took it. Their big splash was trading for Jaylen Waddle, a hugely underrated receiver who saw his production dip last year when Tua Tagovailoa imploded. It cost them a first and a third—they also swapped fourths with Miami—but he and Courtland Sutton give quarterback Bo Nix an excellent #1 and #2. They otherwise focused on retaining their own talent on both sides of the ball and used limited draft capital—their first pick was in the third round—on the trenches, at tight end, and picking up a bruising runner in Jonah Coleman for a crowded group of backs. They’re likely to once again be a major contender in the AFC, barring a meltdown from Nix. What to know about Friday As always, this is a good opportunity to see how Falcons’ starters stack up against the starters on a really quality football team, and what their depth looks like against equivalent players outside of the roster. Thus far we’ve seen a lot of encouraging things from the defense in camp and some sharp performances from quarterbacks and receivers for the Falcons offense, but will they maintain that against Denver? I look forward to finding out. The fact that the Falcons will indeed give their starters some run after Arthur Smith largely eschewed that and Raheem Morris completely avoided doing so will be refreshing, even if it’s only likely to be for a small handful of snaps. Otherwise, what we’re looking for is A) the team exiting this game in good health and B) some movement in the various roster battles we’ve been tracking to this point. I’m particularly excited to see rookies Zachariah Branch and Avieon Terrell in action, and to get a glimpse at how Christian Harris, Kendal Daniels, and Harold Perkins Jr. look at inside linebacker, a position that is fraught with uncertainty with Divine Deablo’s injury history and Kaden Ellis’s departure. We’ll have plenty to talk about over the weekend.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: tackle/guard Jude Bowry
summary: The Buffalo Bills under general manager Brandon Beane have done a good job building offensive line depth. Beane has a type, too, as he often takes shots at very athletic pieces up front who have the athleticism to play at multiple positions. If you’re going to be a backup offensive lineman in Buffalo, you need […]
full_text: Bills offensive lineman Chase Lundt holds off the pressure from Jude Bowry during the final day of Buffalo Bills training camp at St. John Fisher University Friday, August 7, 2026 in Pittsford. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Buffalo Bills under general manager Brandon Beane have done a good job building offensive line depth. Beane has a type, too, as he often takes shots at very athletic pieces up front who have the athleticism to play at multiple positions. If you’re going to be a backup offensive lineman in Buffalo, you need to know how to play multiple positions. That isn’t an official mantra for the club, but it’s proven to be a philosophy they follow throughout the last few years. Even if a player has limited experience at a secondary position, the Bills will often cross-train their reserves to give themselves greater flexibility with the active roster on Sundays. In today’s installment of “91 players in 91 days, we discuss a rookie offensive lineman who likely won’t contribute much this year, but who could make a push for time in 2027 and beyond. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Jude Bowry Number: 74 Position: T/G Height/Weight: 6’5” 314 lbs. Age: 22 (23 on 8/19/2026) Experience/Draft: R; selected by Buffalo in the fourth round (No. 102 overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft College: Boston College Acquired: Fourth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Bowry’s four-year rookie deal is worth a total of $5,720,744 overall. For the 2026 season, his cap hit is $1,203,936 if he makes the 53-man roster. Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $1,275,744 if he’s released. 2025 Recap: Bowry missed three games due to injury during his final NCAA campaign, but overall, he was an important member of the Eagles’ offense. He was the starting left tackle for the second consecutive season, but for the first time, Bowry was also named team captain. Under head coach Bill O’Brien, BC was just 2-10 last season, averaging 25.4 points per game on offense. Bowry accepted an invite to play in the 2026 Panini Senior Bowl. At the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine, he tested quite well overall, posting a 34.5” vertical, a 9’7” broad jump, and a 5.08-second forty-yard dash. At BC’s Pro Day, he completed 24 reps of the 225-pound bench press. His 9.40 Relative Athletic Score (RAS) placed him at No. 98 out of 1,606 offensive tackles analyzed since 1987. Positional outlook: Bowry and Tylan Grable are both listed at tackle/guard. The other tackles on the current roster are Dion Dawkins, Spencer Brown, Chase Lundt, and Travis Clayton. The other guards on the roster are Ar’Maj Reed-Adams, O’Cyrus Torrence, Connor McGovern, Austin Corbett, Sedrick Van Pran-Granger, Bruno Fina, Da’Metrius Weatherspoon, Nick Broeker, and Alec Anderson. 2026 Offseason: Bowry has worked mostly as the second-team left tackle this summer, but he has taken some first-team reps when Dion Dawkins was out. 2026 Season outlook: Barring injury, Bowry has little chance at earning a starting role this season. Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins are set at right tackle and left tackle, respectively, and while Bowry carries a guard designation on the roster, he has little experience there and has worked mostly at tackle. He’s likely competing for the job as Buffalo’s primary swing tackle right now given that it’s where he played in college and it’s where he’s spent most of his time this summer. That time has been well spent, too, as Bowry’s play has received near-universal positive feedback. Head coach Joe Brady called him a rookie who “doesn’t blink,” among other positives, and Patrick Moran noted that Bowry has outperformed Grable throughout camp practices. Bowry’s draft status made him a likely lock for the roster, but it’s fair to say that his early performance has solidified that thought. Bowry likely will not only make the 53-man roster, but he’ll likely be the active reserve offensive tackle on game days, as well. Last season, Buffalo kept a Day Three rookie offensive tackle in Chase Lundt, but he was often inactive on Sundays. I don’t think Bowry will suffer that same fate, as he’ll likely be one of the eight linemen the team dresses for games. He could see some time as a sixth offensive lineman, if the Bills choose to go that route, but he’ll likely appear only on special teams unless Brown or Dawkins are injured. The real question about Bowry comes after this season, as Dawkins is set to count $25 million against the 2027 salary cap. Could the Bills release Dawkins, save $12 million in doing so, and turn over Josh Allen’s blindside protection to Bowry? For the rookie, that has to be the goal he’s working towards. Just because we don’t expect him to play much in 2026 doesn’t mean that he won’t, however. If you recall, Dawkins was drafted as insurance at tackle, and he was expected to be a reserve as a rookie. However, when starting left tackle Cordy Glenn suffered a series of injuries, Dawkins stepped into the role and never looked back. Jude Bowry likely won’t start this season, but if he does, it seems that the head coach thinks he has what it takes to play well if the need arises. He’s a rookie to watch once preseason action begins.

title: Buffalo Bills cosplay: Final paint and more, breastplate
summary: We’re getting closer and closer to a full set of Mandalorian armor decked out in Buffalo Bills flair. I’ve got final paint on the leg and shoulder pieces, the helmet was revealed early thanks to the Bills themselves copying my design and forcing my hand. I made some promises along the way though, and I […]
full_text: We’re getting closer and closer to a full set of Mandalorian armor decked out in Buffalo Bills flair. I’ve got final paint on the leg and shoulder pieces, the helmet was revealed early thanks to the Bills themselves copying my design and forcing my hand. I made some promises along the way though, and I can’t be done without coming through on them. One of those gets revealed today, with what I believe is an upgrade on the original idea. The Paint You’re seen it with the beskar look before, now it’s time to reveal the paint design. That’s arguably the least intriguing part of the reveal on this, but I hope still pretty good. Most of the armor has been a base coat of blue and I decided to keep that. Remember though that the helmet is the Sabine Wren one, a notable graffiti artist. I couldn’t leave it with just the blue. That said, I didn’t want it to be as elaborate as the tassets and spaulders either. When I did the ombre design on the blaster, I hinted I might work to make this piece match, and that did become the inspiration. I’ll stop chatting and just show you my “Bills Nebula” design. The center decorative element didn’t come out as clean as I hoped, but fits the “kinda beat up” look it has pretty well (but yeah, this is a tiny disappointment). I’m also deliberately hiding the full view of it for now, so you can’t see the Batman elements I integrated for shaping the plates. We have a tangent to go on first. Promises Promise made Way, way back in the series I discussed the helmet design. The vertical charge, which is much nicer than the thick horizontal version (cough, cough), was completed as promised. I originally wanted a design on the opposite side and promised this. To be fair, I hinted that the promise was a GOOD version of this. This was the initial concept and testing of the Frog Tape for stenciling. Do you remember what this is? It’s a cross between a bison skull and the mythosaur logo from the Mandalorian. When I got the charge stripe on the helmet I felt it looked… right. Just the way it was. I decided not to paint the bison/mythosaur on the helmet. In fact, I decided not to paint it at all. Promise kept But make no mistake, I didn’t abandon it. I improved it. I’d like to think that through all of this I’ve put a stake in the gound as an “acceptable” level painter with a spray can. Heck, maybe even “not too shabby.” There’s one skill though I’ll abandon any pretense of humility over and that’s wood carving. Have you seen my wood and steel miniatures? I kept my fingertips in for scale. If you’re not sure what any of these are and want to take a peek at how I might have done, they are: Great Scythe from Dark Souls Blade of Mercy from Bloodborne Geralt’s twin swords from The Witcher (some show and game elements blended together) Squall’s gunblade from Final Fantasy VIII The Soul Reaver from the Legacy of Kain/Blood Omen series I figured if I can whittle wood, why not plastic. How’d I do? pic.twitter.com/ZaIuo5CQe8 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) August 12, 2026 There’s the nebula paint, batman-inspired plate shapes, and the final bison/mythosaur hybrid. I could have done it more 3D, but wanted it look more like a pin or welded on insignia. Here’s a shot of it directly in case you don’t want to pause the video. You might have noticed two things. That the eyes seem to be cut all the way through and that there’s a white plastic silhouette behind it. Here’s a hint, the white plastic is there to disperse light. title: Ranking likeliest Brandon Beane August Trade candidates on Buffalo Bills roster
summary: Brandon Beane loves himself an August trade. It started with Sammy Watkins, Ronald Darby, and Reggie Ragland in his first August as Bills GM. Others since include Eli Harold for Ryan Bates, sending Wyatt Teller to the Browns, and netting late-round selections for the likes of Corey Coleman, Russell Bodine, Darryl Johnson, Boogie Basham, and […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: DeWayne Carter #90 of the Buffalo Bills embraces the rain during a break in drills during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brandon Beane loves himself an August trade. It started with Sammy Watkins, Ronald Darby, and Reggie Ragland in his first August as Bills GM. Others since include Eli Harold for Ryan Bates, sending Wyatt Teller to the Browns, and netting late-round selections for the likes of Corey Coleman, Russell Bodine, Darryl Johnson, Boogie Basham, and Cody Ford. Beane did not make an August trade in 2025, which means he’s due. Let’s list the players most likely to be traded by Beane in the coming weeks before the start of the 2026 regular season. The players are listed from least likely to most likely Keon Coleman Coleman has to be mentioned here as the former first pick in the second round — of the 2024 NFL Draft — who has clearly underperformed entering Year 3. His inclusion can further be explained simply by the sped-up nature of today’s NFL and because he hasn’t locked down the WR3 role on this team after a very quiet camp. The Bills have said nothing to indicate Coleman is on the trade block. But of course not every traded player was once situated on the trade block. If Coleman plays a lot during the preseason — which I fully expect him to — and hardly makes an impact, you will likely hear his name mentioned in trade speculation. Now, the Bills roster doesn’t feature a surplus of receiver talent, and the team is unlikely to abandon an early second-round pick before his third season even begins, but Coleman has his work cut out for him to become a serviceable piece of Joe Brady’s offense. Lloyd Cushenberry Looks like Cushenberry, not Sedrick Van Pran-Granger whom I gave the nod to at backup center on my most recent 53-man roster projection , took first-team snaps at center this week with Connor McGovern dinged, so as it currently stands, Cushenberry is an unlikely trade chip. However, his experience — which was likely integral to the Bills signing him — would be enticing to other clubs who may be in dire need on the interior of their offensive line as the regular season approaches. Theoretically, Cushenberry would hold reasonable trade value. Yet given McGovern’s injury, it feels even unlikely the Bills trade a center at this stage. And, like other clubs, the Bills almost assuredly love his 80 games of regular-season starting experience. Plus, Cushenberry was Brady’s center during the famous 2019 season at LSU. Damar Hamlin It feels quite obvious that Hamlin and Geno Stone are in a one-on-one battle to be the Bills veteran insurance policy at safety behind starters Cole Bishop and Chauncey Gardner-Johnson in a room that now features springy youngsters Jalon Kilgore and Jordan Hancock. From my watch, Hamlin had one of his better training camps, which of course helps his candidacy to simply make the Bills 53-man roster after the preseason. Plus, there is some leadership to his presence on the team. Yet, if the club ultimately deems him the loser of the backup veteran safety battle, he could be moved for a late-round selection in one of the next two drafts. Geno Stone Stone was added early in free agency as a deep depth option with loads of experience at the safety position. He’s always felt like someone who could be thrust into a legitimate backup role or not make the team out of camp. Given the presence of Hancock and Kilgore — who offer more versatility — along with Gardner-Johnson avoiding serious injury at training camp, Stone isn’t a lock to be on the 53 right now. Far from. And he had a fine albeit very unspectacular showing at St. John Fisher University. If the club likes the familiarity with Hamlin (although it’s a new defensive staff) and Stone is simply outplayed by him in the preseason, this former Bengals and Ravens safety feels like someone who Beane would dangle in trade talks before September. Sedrick Van Pran-Granger SVPG is more likely to be moved than Cushenberry because of his positioning behind Cushenberry on the team’s depth chart ahead of the preseason opener against the Panthers. A 2024 fifth-round pick, SVPG has been groomed as a developmental blocker after an illustrious career at the pivot for national title winning Georgia Bulldogs teams. Now would the be time for Van Pran-Granger to grab the emergency starter gig — with McGovern sidelined — but apparently that hasn’t happened yet. I included Cushenberry and SVPG together because it feels like the odd-man out at backup center will either be traded or released. Or at least there’s a strong likelihood of either of those transactions when the backup center battle concludes. The winner could possibly start Week 1. DeWayne Carter Carter hardly made a blip on the radar as a rookie in 2024 — he started as a healthy scratch — before a torn Achilles derailed his second professional season before it began. Now he’s apparently bulked up in the 330 range to morph into a rotational nose tackle, not exactly a spot on the roster that holds extreme position value to begin with. However, nose tackles tend to need breaks throughout the game / season, so if Carter were to make waves in the preseason, he could sell himself as an important piece behind Deone Walker. However, to date, Carter has hardly popped. I noticed one tackle close to the line in training camp. And with an entirely new defensive staff not tied to his draft selection in 2024, I firmly believe he has an uphill climb to make the roster. He was drafted to be a one-gap penetrator weighing around 300 pounds. Now he’s being asked to take on an entirely new, two-gapping, dirty-work role with drastically altered body composition. Although, given he’s only 25 with a clean bill of health, it wouldn’t be shocking if another team would be interested in sending the Bills a late-rounder to acquire his services.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: running back Ray Davis
summary: Last season the Buffalo Bills employed the NFL’s leading rusher. That’s the first time that happened since O.J. Simpson was carrying the football in 1976. With that kind of output from your top running back, opportunities for any of the reserve rushers are obviously going to be limited. The Bills had a pretty clear hierarchy […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Ray Davis #7 and DeWayne Carter #90 high five during the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last season the Buffalo Bills employed the NFL’s leading rusher. That’s the first time that happened since O.J. Simpson was carrying the football in 1976. With that kind of output from your top running back, opportunities for any of the reserve rushers are obviously going to be limited. The Bills had a pretty clear hierarchy at the position last season, as each of the team’s top three running backs fit into particular roles. Arguably, all three of the players thrived in those roles, even if they weren’t all exactly thrilled about the opportunities they had. In today’s installment of our “91 players in 91 days” series, we discuss one of the Bills’ backup running backs, a player who made a name for himself in a completely different area last season. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Ray Davis Number: 7 Position: RB Height/Weight: 5’8” 220 lbs. Age: 26 (27 on 11/11/2026) Experience/Draft: 3; selected by Buffalo in the fourth round (No. 128 overall) of the 2024 NFL Draft College: Kentucky Acquired: Fourth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Davis enters the third year of his four-year rookie contract, which is worth $4,733,188 overall. For the 2026 season, his cap hit is $1,253,297 if he’s on the 53-man roster, and the Bills will carry a dead cap charge of $356,594 if they release him. 2025 Recap: After a solid rookie campaign as the second back behind James Cook, Davis looked primed to take another step forward in his second season. However, he was next to a nonfactor on offense for much of the year, and he saw double-figures in carries just once. That was during Buffalo’s regular-season finale, a blowout win over the New York Jets in which they were resting most of their starters. Davis carried 21 times for 151 yards in that game, adding two receptions for 23 yards and a score to his ledger. Given that, for the whole season, Davis had 58 rushes for 275 yards and 10 receptions for 86 yards with two touchdowns, that final game stands as a major outlier on what was otherwise pedestrian production offensively. Much of that was due to lack of opportunity that sprung from James Cook having a career year, which led him to stay on the field more often than he had in 2024. It wasn’t a wasted year for Davis, though, as he instead emerged as the top kickoff return man in the league. He averaged an NFL-best 30.4 yards per kickoff return, taking 31 tries for 943 yards and a touchdown. In the playoffs, he led the NFL in kickoff return attempts (9) and kickoff return yards (249) despite the Bills playing in only two postseason games. For his efforts, Davis earned First-Team All-Pro recognition as a kickoff returner, becoming the first Buffalo player to earn such an honor in team history. Terrence McGee was named Second-Team All-Pro as a returner twice, in both the 2004 and 2005 seasons, but he never earned the First-Team nod like Davis did last year. Positional outlook: Davis is one of five running backs on the roster. Ian Wheeler, James Cook III, Ty Johnson, and Frank Gore Jr. are the others. Ben VanSumeran and Jackson Acker are listed at fullback. 2026 Offseason: Davis is healthy, though he did go through an injury scare at a practice on August 4. He has participated since, however, and he is on track for the start of the preseason. 2026 Season outlook: It’s fair to wonder what Davis’ role will be this season, and in his own words, he wants to have a bigger role in 2026 than he did in 2025 . I can’t say I’m mad at him—I’ve always said that I’d rather have a player working hard who wants the ball over someone who’s content to do less, and so long as that player isn’t being a distraction for the group, I’ll take the competitor every time. Davis has been a consummate pro in his two seasons with the Bills, accepting a smaller role on offense last season and making the most of his opportunity on special teams. In short bursts, he’s proven himself to be more than capable of handing the majority of backfield duties, as well. His issue isn’t his own ability, it’s that he plays on a team that employ a running back who happens to be one of the best in the NFL. Could Davis slot in as RB2 like he did as a rookie? Some of that might depend on Ty Johnson’s health, as the veteran suffered a hamstring injury during the Return of the Blue and the Red scrimmage. While it’s not expected to cause him to miss regular season time, hamstrings are tricky; those are the kind of injuries that tend to linger. While that might be a great Cranberries song, it’s not something we want for Ty Johnson moving forward, so the Bills might choose to give him closer to the maximum recovery time of four weeks rather than rushing him back in two. That could open the door for Davis to see some increased opportunity in the early going. I assume that Cook is going to remain on the field for close to 60% of the offensive snaps like he did last season, so there isn’t a ton of opportunity for Davis, but he’s shown himself to be a dangerous receiver out of the backfield, and he can carry the load if needed. At worst, we’re looking at a great RB3 who has become a truly elite kickoff returner. At best, we’re looking at a strong RB2 who could make an argument for being the second part of a committee approach on many other teams who lack a star running back. In short, Davis might be disappointed if he expects a tremendous increase in his offensive workload this season, but the Bills could give him some more touches in the early going to the benefit of both the player and the team. Davis is a great insurance policy and a very good back overall.

title: Panthers vs Bills: Defensive Preview
summary: Hello CSR! We’re into week 1 (technically) of the preseason as the Panthers will play their first game with some starters mixing in. The Bills also intend to mix some of their starters in, but whether both teams play an equal number of snaps with their starters is always a toss up during the preseason. […]
full_text: Dec 21, 2025; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Carolina Panthers safety Lathan Ransom (22) celebrates the game-winning interception against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second half at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images Hello CSR! We’re into week 1 (technically) of the preseason as the Panthers will play their first game with some starters mixing in. The Bills also intend to mix some of their starters in, but whether both teams play an equal number of snaps with their starters is always a toss up during the preseason. The Bills don’t really have much to prove on offense as an annual playoff contender, while the Panthers could potentially play starters a little bit longer as a team on the upswing, with question marks. Let’s dive into the Panthers defense vs the Bills offense! Important snaps for EDGE Princely Umanmielen The Panthers signed Jaelan Phillips to be their top edge guy, and have Patrick Jones returning from injury slated as their starters. Jones was held out of practice Wednesday with what the team called an “illness”, but regardless of that I’d expect both those players not to play more than a handful of snaps. However, Princely Umanmielen is slated to have an opportunity as the team’s primary designated pass rusher, and I think they give him a lot more snaps in this game than the top two. Getting Princely out in front of the Bills starting (or close to starting) offensive line should be a great status check on where his development is at. He’s the guy I’m excited to see the most on defense. Inside Linebacker competition Dave Canales announced this week that the ILB spot next to 2026 free agent acquisition Devin Lloyd was currently a competition between 2024 3rd round pick Trevin Wallace and 2023 UDFA acquisition Claudin Cherelus. I don’t think Lloyd will play a ton either, probably will end up off the field once the set in stone starters are done getting their reps in. However, this competition is very important for the Panthers, as that 2nd linebacker spot will matter in both base defenses and in nickel packages calling for two linebackers in coverage. In theory, this job was Wallace’s to lose, but between inconsistent play and injury, the guy who has filled in many times in Wallace’s absence has a strong chance to take the job. Both should have plenty of chances to make plays in the passing game and rushing game on Saturday. Lathan Ransom gets another shot to shine Ransom has been one of the highlights of the preseason, consistently laying the wood and making hits from his safety position. Fans have often called for him to be the starter next to Tre’Von Moehrig, and while I have said all off-season Nick Scott isn’t going anywhere, Ransom is certainly making me sweat in my special teams ace boots. Ransom should get a ton of time with the 1s and 2s as a starter, and this is his time to show it. What are you looking for from the defense on Sunday, Panthers fans?

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 31 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: 8 Oct 2000: Eric Davis #25 of the Carolina Panthers gets ready to move at the snap during the game against the Seattle Seahawks at the Ericsson Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. The Panthers defeated the Seahawks 23-3.Mandatory Credit: Scott Halleran /Allsport | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #31. Eric Davis Eric Davis followed up a quality college career at Jacksonville State by being the 53rd overall pick in the 1990 NFL Draft selected by the San Francisco 49ers. After playing a lot but not starting his rookie season, he won the starting job in his second year only to miss most of the year after a severe shoulder injury in just the second game of the season. Despite the setback, Davis returned the following year with a vengeance, starting all 16 games while notching 61 tackles and three interceptions. After helping the 49ers claim the Super Bowl in the 1995 season and being named a First Team All-Pro, he left as an unrestricted free agent. He signed a four year, $11.4 million deal with the Panthers, which is the equivalent of about $21 million per year in today’s salary cap (think DaRon Bland, AJ Terrell type of contract). Davis spent five seasons with the Panthers overall and was outstanding every year. The 1996 season was his second Pro Bowl year in a row as Davis had 60 tackles and five picks while forcing three fumbles for the surprise NFC Championship runner ups. Davis was incredibly consistent turning the ball over with Carolina, snagging exactly five interceptions every season during his five year tenure. Passes defended didn’t become an official stat until 1999, and that really showed Davis’s impact on the game. He had 24 passes defended in 1999, good for second in the NFL and only one off the leader. He followed that up with 18 the following year, even adding four forced fumbles for good measure. Though the Panthers ended up releasing Davis following the 2000 season, he played a couple more years in the league with the Broncos and Lions before retiring. Eric Davis is one of several players we all look back fondly on from those late 90s Panthers teams. Up until some guy named Chris Gamble, Davis was the franchise leader in career interceptions. Further cementing his impact: Davis got 25 picks in five seasons, while Gamble needed eight years to get his 27. That 1996 squad had some dawgs on it, as GM Dan Morgan would say, and Eric Davis was right there in the middle of that pack, earning his spot at No.31 on our list.

summary: Chicago Bears president Kevin Warren and chairman George McCaskey met with the media Thursday afternoon for their annual preseason briefing. Following his usual opening remarks of complimentary platitudes, his actual remarks […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 04: President of the Chicago Bears, Kevin Warren looks on before the game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on January 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Chicago Bears president Kevin Warren and chairman George McCaskey met with the media Thursday afternoon for their annual preseason briefing. While unfounded reports on X, the everything app, suggest today would be the big, huge announcement we’ve all been waiting for, it was not. Following his usual opening remarks of complimentary platitudes, his actual remarks on the stadium really didn’t amount to much. Warren reported a “record” revenue last year for the team. He says that Soldier Field has added new in-stadium suites, “RVs” fans can reserve for a game. But as for the stadium update, Warren says the ‘sole focus’ is on Hammond right now. Key quotes: “Working with Indiana officials on the capital stack and financing.” “Due diligence is going on at the Wolf Lake terminal site and it’s finished at the Lost Marsh site. They’ve identified another site” The other site is the terminal site. Regarding a potential site for a Bears stadium in Hammond, Indiana, Kevin Warren says the Bears have completed their "due diligence" at the Lost Marsh site this summer, which is a 'viable' site. While they were evaluating that property, the Bears discovered an opportunity to… — Courtney Cronin (@CourtneyRCronin) August 13, 2026 “We’ve had occasional meetings with the state of Illinois. But at this time our sole focus is on developing a world-class stadium and mixed-use development in Hammond, Ind.” Warren said there have been “occasional” meetings with Illinois, but later said they have been minimal. He also admitted he has not been involved in every meeting with Illinois at this point. My read on it is the NFL lobbyists have taken over most of that. Warren emphasized the fans are at the forefront of all of the decisions and everything that’s being done. “The biggest thing for our fans is we have to get this right. I’m looking forward to bringing it to a close.” Finally, the last real quote of interest came from a question about what he’s learned from the process and if he believes he’s made any mistakes along the way. “I don’t think we’ve made any mistakes. As you look at these projects, I really look at these as learning opportunities.” Kevin Warren on the Bears’ stadium project: “I don’t think we’ve made any mistakes. As you look at these projects, I really look at these as learning opportunities.” — Chris Emma (@ChrisEmma1) August 13, 2026 And while he said that it was important for the team to “move with haste” he would not offer any target dates. He said his wife told him to stop saying target dates publicly. “The target is the right time.” The stadium saga rolls on. Indiana is in the driver’s seat, but to me, I think they’re going to drag it out to see if they can get something in writing with Illinois. Finally, I would say the idea Warren floated of “merging” the Lost Marsh and Wolf Lake Terminal sites- one look at Google Maps says that will be difficult.

title: A Day at Halas Hall
summary: Bryan got to take his wife and two eldest to Bears training camp for the first time for “Women and Girls in Sports Day.” Here are his takeaways. Transportation I stayed at a hotel nearby Halas Hall and it was just a quick shot over to the mall where the free shuttle picked up droves […]
full_text: Bryan got to take his wife and two eldest to Bears training camp for the first time for “Women and Girls in Sports Day.” Here are his takeaways. Transportation I stayed at a hotel nearby Halas Hall and it was just a quick shot over to the mall where the free shuttle picked up droves of fans. There were maybe two dozen parking lot attendants and/or Bears staff and they were all spry and welcoming even at 7:15am. I found it so energizing to arrive to something like this with so many Bears fans. Normally I hate long lines, but this was different. Of course, those of us that have ever attended a home game know what I mean, but my kids had never experienced anything like it. Suddenly my eldest didn’t feel so silly wearing all of her Bears gear or her hat that she feels is too big for her after she got multiple compliments. I was blown away at just how many shuttle busses there were and how efficiently they all operated. Upon arrival to Halas Hall, we were led to the entrance which resembled a theme park instead of a practice facility. A truly special experience from the jump. It was upon entry that I was met with my first challenge. Do I stop at each potential vendor and interactive experience for my kids or do I shoot to the fields to get a good seat closest to action? I chose the latter in a decision that may or may not have come back to bite me. At the conclusion of practice for the day, people spent more time enjoying the festivities and making their way back to the shuttles where we waited in line to get shuttled back to the mall parking lot. A pretty efficient and painless operation – just in time for some lunch. Practice I got to the fields along with the first 100 or so crazy fans and was pleasantly surprised to see multiple covered bleachers along the two fields where practice was being held. There were only a handful of player on the field – most notably Colston Loveland and Jahdae Walker. Along with a few reserve offensive linemen. I gave Jahdae a shout during his stretches/dances and he waived at me. When practice began to start, music was playing and most of the team had already come out to the field by then. My biggest takeaway was just how well-oiled this machine truly was. Most of you know by now that I was a walk-on at UCF in the early 2000’s. That was my first experience with heavily structured practices that wasted zero time between transitions from station to station. Not only were the time periods shown on the clock at the far end of the field, but someone announced over the intercom what station they were transitioning to. The players wasted zero time between transition and I even got to witness a friendly race amongst the WRs where Rome Odunze had fun beating his teammates to where the WRs and QBs were going to be practicing. Caleb Williams looks every bit the part of the face of the franchise. Now in a contrived, obligatory was like former 1st round QBs have appeared – but one that has the respect of his teammates, coaches, staff and fans. He demands excellence, celebrates small victories and holds others and himself accountable. His energy was palpable from the moment he stepped onto the field and it rubbed off on his teammates throughout practice. I was forced to leave practice a bit early to check out some of the stuff we passed by before it was too late and then did our best to position ourselves for autographs. Festivities Again, this was a day catered towards women and girls and it did not disapoint. Face painting, pinwheel games, pictures with Staley and various interactive stations along with ample food and drink food trucks and places to sit. A bit much for the “inner-scout” in me, but absolutely worthwhile if you are bringing children. We even got to attend an autograph session inside the Walter Payton center which was super fun for the kids. One of my daughters got Anthony Johnson Jr. and Beau Gardner and the other got Josh Blackwell and Cairo Santos. The experience was made complete with music, food, and good vibes – all catered towards kids and women. And it was a great first-impression for my daughters to see that football isn’t just some boring hobby that their daddy obsesses over 24/7. No, in fact, there are thousands of crazy obsessed Bears fans all over and together we can marvel at what Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams are doing for The Beloved. Bear Down. Check out Ryan Droste and I discuss some takeaways from camp and other Bears related items whilst sharing a cold beverage.
