title: Where does J.J. McCarthy Go from Here?
summary: When Kevin O’Connell and the Minnesota Vikings announced that Kyler Murray would start in Week 1 over incumbent(ish) J.J. McCarthy, it unleashed a stream of takes ranging from “least surprising news ever” to “this is a traitorous offense!” You can pretty much guess who the usual suspects were for each reaction, but to say the […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 01: J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during Training Camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 01, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Kevin O’Connell and the Minnesota Vikings announced that Kyler Murray would start in Week 1 over incumbent(ish) J.J. McCarthy, it unleashed a stream of takes ranging from “least surprising news ever” to “this is a traitorous offense!” You can pretty much guess who the usual suspects were for each reaction, but to say the fallout wasn’t uniform is probably more than fair. But what does the future hold for McCarthy, who has played just 519 snaps entering his third NFL season? Is that future in Minnesota, or elsewhere? We asked the experts from Daily Norseman in our latest edition of the roundtable: Was the J.J. McCarthy vs. Kyler Murray battle real ? Brandon Warne : I think it came down to whether Murray showed up even semi-prepared/plugged in or not. He did, and he’s the starter. Craig Williams : I don’t believe it was. It appeared to me that Kevin O’Connell had already turned the page in his mind prior to camp. Warren Ludford : It was a competition, but not between equals. Dave Stefano : Sort of. Sam Buegler : I don’t know if I would call it a competition, but more of a race, with Kyler having 70 percent odds and J.J. having 30 percent. If yes, was it fair? BW : I don’t know about “fair” or “unfair.” McCarthy’s injury luck is far more unfair to him than anything O’Connell and Co. have thrown at him so far. The “forced to back up” tweet from Adam Schefter was hilarious, I might add. I think the writing was on the wall the second Murray was signed. And beyond that, one of the adages I hold closely no matter WL : Murray has already developed the skill set necessary to be a quality starter, and McCarthy has not. I think KOC was trying to give some respect and motivation to McCarthy by going with a competition rather than naming Murray the starter outright when he was signed. But given the difference in skill sets, it was a race equivalent to a 40-yard dash with Murray having a head start at the 20. DS : I say sort of because when the Vikings signed Kyler Murray, it was to motivate J.J. McCarthy. They needed to see a huge jump in his performance and processing, and even though there was a jump due to his offseason training and coaching, it wasn’t enough in the collective’s mind. The collective is the decision-makers, of which Kevin O’Connell is but one. SB : Sure, J.J. had a chance to start, but it was more of a long shot if Kyler ended up not being what they hoped for. But I think that McCarthy knew that going into it. It was the unspoken thing throughout training camp, but they wouldn’t have brought in the former first overall pick if not to start. The overall fairness of the competition favored the media, even if there was an element of truth to it. Where do you stand, at present, on McCarthy’s future as an NFL quarterback? BW : I still believe there’s a solid starter in there. Or at the very least, I still believe we have no idea what his trajectory looks like. Again, he’s played just over 500 snaps — and they all come with a condition of “he’s functionally a rookie/he’s knocking off rust.” Anyone who acts like they’re certain, at least in my opinion, is having a hot take just to have a hot take. CW : He’s one hit away from starting again, so it’s hard to count him out. He’s young and has a chance to develop. I could easily see him coming back like Sam Darnold. WL : Odds and history don’t look favorable for McCarthy to become a quality starter in the future. The light could still come on, but there aren’t many examples like McCarthy to date eventually becoming a quality starter. DS : I feel McCarthy will continue to develop into a starting QB with the right coaching and surroundings. SB : Right now, I think he could be solid. He needs time to work on his mentality and poise, but he showed enough flashes to make me believe he might still have a career as a solid starter or a good backup. I would love to be proven wrong and blown away, but I think all the media attention, pressure, and memes have just rattled him. He needs a bit of time out of the spotlight to develop and come back stronger. Will McCarthy take another regular-season snap with the Vikings? BW : Yes, I think he will. CW : No, I believe the Vikings move on from J.J. McCarthy and give Wentz the backup role. WL: It’s possible McCarthy takes another snap for the Vikings if Murray is injured, and if he isn’t traded, he could still win the starting job next year, but that seems like a long shot at this point. DS : As of now, yes. SB : Yes. If yes, when? BW : Sooner rather than later, I think. There are just too many durability concerns with Murray. In fact, between Murray, McCarthy and Carson Wentz, you have a solid “see no evil/hear no evil/speak no evil” trifecta at quarterback. DS : Sometime this season. As of now, he is QB2 behind a QB1 who also has an injury history. It is very hard for a starting QB to stay healthy enough to start and play all 17 regular season games (only about a third or less of teams have that happen). SB : I do think he will have to come in, maybe not for a start or a full game, but I do believe that Kyler will have to come out at some point and J.J. will need to play for a drive or two or more. Probably not right away, maybe after Week 8, but I do believe he will have to play. Or – depending on how the season plays out – he could start Week 18. Give him a chance to prove how he has developed and matured. That is only if we are secure in the standings, whether for good or bad reasons; we don’t know. If not, who will his next regular-season snap be with? CW : The Chargers will get a lot of buzz for a potential landing spot. I like the Buccaneers, Dolphins, or the Patriots as potential spots as well. He won’t compete for a starting role, but he’ll be on a roster. Given the way the league works, he’ll likely get at least a few snaps for an injury, a concussion check, or garbage time. WL : It’s anybody’s guess at this point where McCarthy may land in a trade or after his contract expires next year. If traded, maybe a trade with the Colts for Anthony Richardson, with hopes on both sides that a change of scenery will help their development. Otherwise, after his contract expires, maybe going to the Chargers as a backup to Herbert under Jim Harbaugh.
author: David Stefano

title: What we learned from Patriots’ preseason tie with the Colts
summary: The New England Patriots played the opening game of their 2026 preseason against the visiting Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. It might have been a relatively uneventful game ending in a 13-13 tie, but there was still a lot to see and take away from. Some guys seemingly helped themselves, while others had a tough time. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: John Saunders Jr. #23 of the New England Patriots celebrates his interception with his teammates during a game between the New England Patriots and the Indianapolis Colts on August 13, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots played the opening game of their 2026 preseason against the visiting Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. It might have been a relatively uneventful game ending in a 13-13 tie , but there was still a lot to see and take away from. Some guys seemingly helped themselves, while others had a tough time. Let’s sort through all of it and get into our takeaways from the first game of the season. Andy Borregales struggles Andy Borregales has looked great in training camp, but his practice performance did not translate to the field on Thursday. He hit two field goals from 40 and 52 yards, but also missed from quite badly from 55 as well as from 56 and then from 49 at the end of the game to win. He was solid, and clutch, last year, but his first game as a sophomore was rough. The hope is that he gets the misses out of his system, but it was a really bad night for the second-year kicker. Maybe Julian Ashby being hurt and having to work with a backup long snapper hurt the operation, but, they’re professionals, so those misses still shouldn’t happen. I’m not panicking just yet, and neither seems to be head coach Mike Vrabel , but he missed a few field goals during this week’s joint practice, and then missed three on Thursday. That’s not good, and honestly surprising based on what we have seen out of him for most of the summer so far. Injury concerns arise In preseason, you want to see what guys have, get everyone ready to play regular season football, and hopefully come out unscathed on the injury front. The Patriots didn’t manage to accomplish the latter on Thursday. In the first quarter, Ben Brown, who is their top interior backup offensive lineman, went down with an injury . He went from the blue tent to the locker room, which isn’t a good sign. Then, later in the game, Andrew Rupcich got banged up as well even though he remained on the sideline and later gave the all-clear in the locker room. Still, losing two guys at a position where there was already minimal depth is a tough break for the Patriots. The hope is that neither injury is overly serious. Depth O-linemen look good Even though the depth along the offensive line took a hit on Thursday night when Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich got hurt, I liked what I saw from two depth tackles. Both Marcus Bryant, who played early in the game, and Dametrious Crownover, who played late in the game, had pretty solid games. There’s probably only one spot after Will Campbell, Morgan Moses and Caleb Lomu at tackle, and right now Bryant should have the clear edge, but Crownover looked competent out there too (albeit against worse competition). I wonder if this performance gets him some run with the second unit to see if he can handle himself with them. Either way, for a position group that just got hit by injury, and already had a ton of questions on the interior, it was nice to at least see a few of the depth tackles register solid performances. Tommy DeVito has his ups and downs Second-string quarterback Tommy DeVito got the start for the Patriots, and had flashes where he looked very good, like his long pass to Cam Dorner that was wiped off because of a penalty, and the touchdown and curl route passes to Kyle Williams. He also missed a bunch of throws as well, including what should have been a deep TD to Williams, which he left short. Ultimately, his inconsistency is why he is a backup in the first place, and shouldn’t surprise anyone. That said, he has looked good in camp, so I was thinking that he might have a more consistent night. He’s still a fine backup, but I would be worried if… you know what, never mind, I’m not even going to write those words down. Penalties are a concern On multiple occasions, big plays were wiped off the board because of ineligible man downfield penalties. One, came against rookie OT Caleb Romu and was a little suspect because he was engaged in a block, while the other was called against guard James Hudson. There were a bunch of other penalties on the offense as well, including a holding call on Lorenz Metz in the fourth quarter. Overall, the Patriots finished the day with five accepted penalties for a loss of 35 yards. It is something that they are going to have to fix moving forward. Obviously, they played mostly backups, but you still expect better. Two depth edges flash It is no secret that the Patriots need more help rushing the passer from the edge, and the play of Jesse Luketa and Bradyn Swinson should be a bright spot for the Patriots. Both looked explosive and pressured the Colts’ quarterbacks multiple times; one of Swinson’s disruptions led to a John Saunders Jr. interception, and one of Luketa’s led to a sack by Joshua Farmer. The edge room has a few spots up for grabs, and those two looking good could help at least one of them grab a roster spot. John Saunders Jr. has a really solid performance Safety is another of the spots where the Patriots don’t seem to have a ton of quality depth, but John Saunders Jr. had a nice night. He had multiple run stops, an interception with a good return, and also was credited with a forced fumble when he knocked the ball out at the goal line. It might not have been an actual fumble, but the refs missed it, and the Patriots benefitted from a heads-up play. While Saunders Jr. still appears to be on the outside looking in as far as the 53-man team is concerned. More performances like Thursday’s might help him with his case to get one of the depth spots, though. Cameron Dorner keeps showing up The Patriots have a treasure trove of wide receivers including undrafted rookie Cameron Dorner, who has made plays every day of camp. Thursday night was no different. Dorner didn’t get a ton of opportunities, seeing just three total passes thrown his way. He had a really nice catch on one of those targets that was called back because of a penalty. On the very next play, he caught a screen for a first down. Dorner only had one other target, where the defender made a good play on a back-shoulder throw that came in a little high, but what we saw from him was solid. I thought it was also notable that he barely played in the second half, meaning that it looks like he might be a tier ahead of the receivers that were playing with third-string passer Behren Morton. His path to the roster is hard to see, but it’s only because of all the guys ahead of him. If he continues his strong play, there’s a chance that someone else will pick him up if he ends up on waivers. Running back depth is looking good The Patriots put Terrell Jennings on season-ending injured reserve ahead of Thursday’s game, which means that the RB3 job is now fully up for grabs. Jam Miller, Lan Larison, and newcomers JaMichael Hasty and Hassan Haskins all looked pretty good at times versus Indianapolis. Miller and Haskins are your more bruising backs, and the Patriots do seem to want that, but Larison and Hasty both run hard as well, and are threats in the passing game while also returning kicks. Time will tell who ends up taking that third spot — although my money is on Miller or Larison — but there was no clear winner in the race on Thursday night. The A.J. Brown Bowl awaits With the first preseason game in the books, the Eagles are set to come to town next week for two joint practices, and then obviously the game next Saturday night. I would imagine that those two practices, which happen on Wednesday and Thursday, Aug. 19 and 20, are going to be absolutely jam-packed. It should be a great opportunity for the Patriots to go against a very good team, and see how good this roster really is. And while preseason games are…

title: 5 winners and losers from Patriots’ preseason tie with the Colts
summary: The New England Patriots opened their preseason Thursday night at Gillette Stadium with a 13-13 tie to the Indianapolis Colts. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ preseason opener. Winners WR Kyle Williams: The second-year receiver got the Patriots their first preseason touchdown as he showcased his talented […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: Kyle Williams #18 of the New England Patriots hauls in a touchdown pass during a game between the New England Patriots and the Indianapolis Colts on August 13, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots opened their preseason Thursday night at Gillette Stadium with a 13-13 tie to the Indianapolis Colts. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ preseason opener. Winners WR Kyle Williams: The second-year receiver got the Patriots their first preseason touchdown as he showcased his talented release package to win off the line of scrimmage before hauling in a 12-yard back shoulder touchdown from Tommy DeVito. Near the end of the half, Williams then kickstarted a drive by working back through contact and then picking up YAC to record a 25-yard drive starter. The speedster then got open on a downfield go route the very next snap for a potential long score but the ball was under-thrown — although Mike Vrabel shared he would have liked Williams to work back to the ball to try and draw defensive pass interference. Either way, Williams showcased his big-play ability and explosive speed that will earn him a role in this offense. Tommy DeVito. Kyle Williams. Automatic. Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bVr8miw3qr — NFL (@NFL) August 14, 2026 TE Eli Raridon: The box score shows a measly one catch on four targets for eight yards for the rookie tight end. But, Raridon had a 24-yard reception where he took off out of the flat on a bootleg concept negated due to an illegal man downfield and had a nice block on the Patriots longest run of the night. Raridon was one the wrong side of other plays in the passing game to hurt his box score but his explosiveness and work in the run game passed the eye test. S John Saunders Jr: As he did to end Tuesday’s joint practice, John Saunders recorded an interception off Riley Leonard deep down the middle of the field. The safety, who drew a start next to Dell Pettus and Mike Brown in the secondary, also tallied a pair of run stuffs Losers K Andy Borregales: New England’s sophomore kicker has enjoyed a strong start to training camp of date, but it was a different story as work transitioned to the preseason. Borregales connected on just 2-of-his-5 field goal attempts with misses from 56, 55, and 49 — the final coming with 13 seconds left in a tie game. “We expect him to make them,” Mike Vrabel said . “That’s pro football. They’re banging them in from 60 yards. They have two kickers on their roster. Andy knows we have to make those field goals.” Guard depth: The Patriots guard depth has been a question mark this summer, and that group got off to a poor start both health and performance wise Thursday night. Top interior backup Ben Brown departed with an injury, although the 28-year old shared he was “OK” in the post game locker room as he walked with a limp but no brace, boot, etc. Andrew Rupcich, who has served as the top option next to Brown, also spent time in the blue medical tent but remained on the sideline. Behind them, both James Hudson and Mehki Butler surrendered sacks. Honorable mentions Top rookies: First-round pick Caleb Lomu played 39 snaps at right tackle in his debut. He allowed just one pressure, but was on scene for a run stuff and was downfield to negate Raridon’s explosive. As for Jacas, the pass rusher tallied a run stuff and helped push the pocket on Kindle Vildor’s early interception. Jacas’ aggressiveness worked against him at times, however, as crashed down to allow a 22-yard read option keeper and 17-yard completion in the flat. Before DeVito’s touchdown to Williams, it was a shaky accuracy night for the QB — in addition to backup Behren Morton — with some sprays. Jam Miller was our winner in the RB3 battle tonight carrying the ball 14 times for 55 yards. Lan Larison did post six catches for 38 yards. Efton Chism III had a crisp 20-yard crossing route on third-down on the Patriots first touchdown drive. Kobe Prentice (3 catches, 40 yards) and Cameron Dorner (1 catch, 18 yards) also flashed in the wide receiver room. Bradyn Swinson logged three pressures in 23 pass rush attempts and had a fourth-down batted pass. He did play into the fourth quarter as Jacas and Quintayvious Hutchins drew the start. LB K.J. Britt had back-to-back impact plays with a two-yard TFL before chasing down Anthony Richardson to force a fumble. Rookie cornerback Karon Prunty blew up a perimeter screen by beating his block.

title: Mike Vrabel provides update on Christian Gonzalez’s recent absence
summary: New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez was among a group of players not in attendance for Thursday’s preseason opener. Gonzalez was also sidelined for Tuesday’s joint practice session with the Indianapolis Colts, marking his first missed practice of the summer. full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 24: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel talks with cornerback Christian Gonzalez on Day 2 of NFL training camp at Gillette Stadium on July 24, 2025. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez was among a group of players not in attendance for Thursday’s preseason opener. Gonzalez was also sidelined for Tuesday’s joint practice session with the Indianapolis Colts, marking his first missed practice of the summer. Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel labeled the absence as a physical issue. “Christian was unavailable, physically unavailable, for the practice. That’s the clarification,“ Vrabel said postgame. ”Just like other players that I told to have treatment, and everybody has a plan here, there were other guys that were in that same category. If you want to list the names, Christian Elliss, Brenden Schooler, Harold Landry, Christian Barmore, et cetera. So, make sure they’re all included. They were all in the same group of what they did.“ Gonzalez ended Monday’s training camp practice taking a hard fall while contending a jump ball against wide receiver Romeo Doubs in the end zone. He appeared to be shaken up following the play but did not appear to suffer a major injury. The 23-year old remains on the middle of contract negotiations with the Patriots as he enters the fourth-year of his rookie contract, with the All-Pro likely ready to reset the cornerback market. After being a limited participant during mandatory minicamp this past spring, Gonzalez has been a full participant in training camp prior to Tuesday.
author: Brian Hines

title: Instant analysis from Patriots’ 13-13 preseason tie against Colts
summary: After three weeks of training camp outside Gillette Stadium, the New England Patriots headed inside. The reigning AFC champions opened the 2026 preseason with a 13-13 tie against the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. Here’s a glance back on the 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff as August moves forward. DeVito drives to halftime as QB2 With […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Tommy DeVito #16 of the New England Patriots passes the ball in the first quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images After three weeks of training camp outside Gillette Stadium, the New England Patriots headed inside. The reigning AFC champions opened the 2026 preseason with a 13-13 tie against the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. Here’s a glance back on the 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff as August moves forward. DeVito drives to halftime as QB2 With 23-year-old captain Drake Maye serving as a spectator for the preseason opener, it would be a waiver claim from last August starting under center for the Patriots. Tommy DeVito went 13-of-22 passing for 138 yards with one touchdown and no turnovers on Thursday night. The former emergency No. 3 quarterback stayed in for six drives against the Colts and was sacked once. Beginning in “22” personnel, with the established Kayshon Boutte and Mack Hollins on the perimeter, the offense’s initial possession brought a 3-0 lead. That was the case despite the latter wide receiver drawing defensive pass interference as a go route for a would-be touchdown hit the turf. A pair of three-and-outs and a missed field goal soon arrived for New England. Yet with 8:22 to go before halftime, so did a play of the night that did not count in the gamebook. Hit high and low by the Colts on first-and-10, DeVito hung in to take a play-action shot. He connected with rookie wideout Cameron Dorner on a 48-yard concentration catch over the top. A penalty for ineligible man downfield took the distance away, only not the work that went into it. The undrafted speedster by way of Shepherd University and North Texas was turned back to on the next snap for a pickup of 17 yards. And that drive, which spanned a dozen snaps, ended in the end zone with second-year target Kyle Williams reeling in a touchdown from a dozen yards away. Rookie quarterback Behren Morton took the keys to New England’s offense after halftime. The Texas Tech product, taken No. 234 overall in the 2026 NFL draft, couldn’t find continuity. He finished 7-of-13 through the air and was taken down for one sack. After three consecutive punts, and score reading 13-13, there was a chance to end on a high note with 1:10 left to go. To no avail. Interior O-line depth thins New England’s first offensive line on the field featured no starters from Super Bowl LX, but a top interior backup in Ben Brown. Thursday night’s starting center had to be helped off the field by trainers after a second-and-7 sack late in the first quarter. Checked on by head coach Mike Vrabel, he went from the blue medical tent to the locker room. And in the final frame, left guard Andrew Rupcich, who spent last year on the practice squad, limped off the field yet stayed on the sideline after further examination in the pop-up. The rest of the Patriots’ starting five included Marcus Bryant at left tackle, James Hudson III at right guard and No. 28 overall pick Caleb Lomu at right tackle. The strong side of the configuration was flagged for roaming downfield, negating completions of 24 yards to tight end Eli Raridon and 48 yards to the aforementioned receiver Cameron Dorner, before their nights closed. The reshuffled line went on to include Mehki Butler, Dametrious Crownover and Jacob Rizy. An unproven range. Seventh-rounder leads the backfield The backfield shakeups continued for the Patriots in the hours leading up to the preseason opener. That was the case as Terrell Jennings, who spent parts of 2024 and 2025 on the 53-man roster, landed on injured reserve in a corresponding move. On Thursday night, the No. 3 conversation went forward even so. Jam Miller started at running back for New England. The No. 245 overall pick via Alabama stayed in to turn 14 handoffs into a team-high 55 rushing yards, led by a long of 15. Spelling the rookie was a redshirt in Lan Larison. After finding the end zone last preseason before going on IR, the UC Davis alum served as a kickoff returner and change of pace with six catches for 38 yards. His ground work, however, resulted in one yard on seven carries. Veteran free agents JaMycal Hasty and Hassan Haskins, who signed following Wednesday workouts, were quickly called upon for five carries apiece. Defensive front serves as a catalyst The Colts got on the board with a QB sneak before intermission hit. But the Patriots got two forced fumbles on the board by then, too. A scramble around the left end saw inside linebacker K.J. Britt jar the football free as defensive tackle Isaiah Iton recovered. And on the subsequent series, down at the goal line, a carry by running back Seth McGowan never crossed the plane from a yard out. It crossed into Jeremiah Pharms Jr. and safety John Saunders Jr. instead. The pair helped turned a touchdown into a turnover. New England’s front included the edge of Gabe Jacas, too. The No. 55 overall pick out of Illinois started opposite Boston College product Quintayvious Hutchins and brought the heat to set up what became the first interception of the preseason for the defense. Not lost in the substitutions was Bradyn Swinson. The 2025 draft choice saw a larger look at outside linebacker to begin the second half. He set the game’s second pick in motion alongside defensive tackle Eric Gregory, and later got his hands up to knock down a fourth-and-3 pass on the doorstep of the end zone. The lone sack of the night would go to fellow sophomore Joshua Farmer for a loss of 12 yards through middle. Pair of picks for the secondary Three passes into the Colts offense’s evening, quarterback Anthony Richardson connected with the Patriots on a tipped ball intended for wideout Coleman Owen. A well-traveled cornerback was there to drive on the route and pick it away through traffic. Vying for a depth spot on the eventual 53-man roster, Kindle Vildor corralled the first interception for New England while starting alongside fifth-round corner Karon Prunty. And at safety, the fumble-forcing John Saunders Jr. got the second on backup QB Riley Leonard under dress after the break. New England’s defensive backfield went with three starting safeties, including Dell Pettus, who fell on a fumble in the shadows of the uprights. Charles Woods as well as 2024 All-Pro and 2025 Pro Bowler Christian Gonzalez did not dress for the exhibition. Wide left three times There were more misses than hits for New England’s operation. From distance, there was also a theme. Andy Borregales converted on 2-of-5 field goals against the Colts. The lone kicker on the Patriots’ 91-man roster began the night with a 40-yarder through the uprights. But a 56-yard launch hooked just outside the left upright as the first quarter closed. And while 2025 draft pick made good on an extra point and then on a 52-yarder coming out of the break, a 55-yard attempt went wide left from there. Then, with 10 seconds left on the clock in a tie game, a 49-yarder followed the same path. As incumbent long snapper Julian Ashby looked on, the Patriots had the recently re-signed Niko Lalos delivering to holder Bryce Baringer.
author: Oliver Thomas

title: Mike Vrabel expresses confidence in Andy Borregales after 3-miss performance
summary: With 10 seconds left in the fourth quarter, Andy Borregales had a chance to break a 13-13 tie and give his team a win in the preseason opener over the Indianapolis Colts. However, the New England Patriots’ place kicker hooked the 49-yard attempt to the left and had to watch the ball sail pass the […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots place kicker Andy Borregales (36) lines up his field goal kick against the Indianapolis Colts during the first half at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect With 10 seconds left in the fourth quarter, Andy Borregales had a chance to break a 13-13 tie and give his team a win in the preseason opener over the Indianapolis Colts. However, the New England Patriots’ place kicker hooked the 49-yard attempt to the left and had to watch the ball sail pass the upright. It wasn’t the first time this happened. Borregales had already missed two of his four previous field goal attempts, sending a 56-yarder and 55-yarder wide to the left in the first and third periods, respectively. After the game, head coach Mike Vrabel was pretty straight-forward in his assessment of the situation. “We expect him to make them,” he said. “That’s pro football. They’re banging them in from 60 yards. They have two kickers on their roster. Andy knows we have to make those field goals.” While Vrabel’s answer was blunt, he did later express confidence in his team’s second-year kicker. “We’re going to have misses, we’re going to have mistakes in everything we do. We just need to be able to come back,” he noted. “We need to be able to bounce back. We need to be able to answer. Guys are going to drop a pass. Guys are going to miss a block. We’re going to miss a kick. We just have to not let those things pile up. “Andy’s been really good with that, and I would anticipate him getting back to work and really start to focus. Maybe it was a footwork thing or trying to over-swing, but I have confidence in Andy. You want to be able to make those. We got in a position to win the football game, and you got to be able to make them.” Borregales joined the Patriots as a sixth-round selection in last year’s draft, and as a rookie won the kicking competition against former practice squad member Parker Romo. However, his career got off to a rocky start: he missed his first career field goal attempt and the following week shanked a couple of extra points. Nonetheless, the Patriots showed trust in him. Borregales kicked a 53-yard game-winning field goal later that same game against the Dolphins, and went on to split the uprights on his next 37 combined attempts. He was a bit more shaky down the stretch but still remained a valuable contributor while making 81.6% of his field goals and 96.8% of his extra points as a rookie.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots lose offensive lineman to injury in preseason opener
summary: The New England Patriots jumped to a 10-7 halftime lead over the Indianapolis Colts in their preseason opener, but they lost a valuable member of their offensive line along the way. Ben Brown, the team’s top backup along the interior O-line, exited the contest after suffering an injury in the second quarter. Starting the game […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JANUARY 04: Ben Brown #77 of the New England Patriots during a game between the New England Patriots and the Miami Dolphins on January 4, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots jumped to a 10-7 halftime lead over the Indianapolis Colts in their preseason opener, but they lost a valuable member of their offensive line along the way. Ben Brown, the team’s top backup along the interior O-line, exited the contest after suffering an injury in the second quarter. Starting the game at center, Brown remained on the ground after a 2-yard sack against quarterback Tommy DeVito. While he did walk off the field under his own power, he required assistance before heading into the blue medical tent on the sideline. After a short stay in the tent, he slowly walked back to the locker room for some further evaluation. Brown, 28, originally arrived in Foxborough during the 2024 season. He spent last year as the Patriots’ fourth interior offensive lineman, starting four games and playing roughly one fourth of offensive snaps on the year. He also signed a two-year, $5 million contract extension in December. The deal cemented his status as the next man up along an interior that enters 2026 led by starting trio Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson and Mike Onwenu. With none of the three taking the field against the Colts, however, Brown was chosen to start the game at center. He was flanked by guards Andrew Rupcich and James Hudson. When he left the game with three minutes left in the first period, undrafted rookie Jacob Rizy took over as New England’s center.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Colts: Final score, stats, game recap from NFL preseason
summary: The New England Patriots opened their preseason on Thursday night, welcoming the Indianapolis Colts to Gillette Stadium. With Drake Maye and most of New England’s regulars set to sit out, the Patriots turned things over to backup quarterback Tommy DeVito to kick things off. With him and the other depth players leading the way, New […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Tommy DeVito #16 of the New England Patriots looks to pass the ball in the first quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots opened their preseason on Thursday night, welcoming the Indianapolis Colts to Gillette Stadium. With Drake Maye and most of New England’s regulars set to sit out, the Patriots turned things over to backup quarterback Tommy DeVito to kick things off. With him and the other depth players leading the way, New England jumped to a 10-7 lead at the half. However, despite, taking the ball away four times on the night, the Patriots failed to build a decisive advantage. This, in turn, allowed Indianapolis to tie the game at 13 apiece in the late fourth quarter. Andy Borregales had a chance to give his team the win on the ensuing drive, but he hooked a 49-yard attempt to the left — his third miss of the day. Final score: Patriots 13 : 13 Colts Thursday, Aug. 13, 7:30 p.m. ET | Gillette Stadium, Foxboro, MA | Broadcast information | Game day roster First Quarter New England won the coin toss and elected to receive to begin the contest. Kicker Andy Borregales capitalized on two defensive pass interferences committed by Indianapolis defensive back Julian Blackmon that set Tommy DeVito’s offense up just outside the red zone. Borregales split the uprights from 40 yards out. [Patriots 3 : 0 Colts] As the Anthony Richardson-led Colts offense looked to respond on their opening drive, a Coleman Owen mishandled pass in the flat ended up in the hands of Patriots cornerback Kindle Vildor. New England’s 2026 free-agency signing was downed by contact at the team’s own 33-yard line. However, after two DeVito incompletions intended for veteran wide receiver Mack Hollins, the Patriots offense quickly went three-and-out. Punter Bryce Baringer then sent a kick 56 yards back to Indianapolis, pinning the opposition inside the ten. Then, shortly after, the Colts quickly traded a punt back to New England. Indianapolis ran a screen, and rookie cornerback Karon Prunty, on 3rd-and-short, forced the receiver inside and into the arms of Channing Canada, who made the stop. The Patriots, taking over at their own 34-yard line, fought their way into Colts territory after two self-inflicted penalties, but a Borregales miss from 56 yards out concluded a scoreless drive to end the first frame. Second Quarter Following a 19-yard completion to Indianapolis wide receiver Nick Westbrook-Ikhine and two Anthony Richardson keepers on the ground, the Colts lined up to snap at the goal line. Despite the pressure, however, Jeremiah Pharms Jr. punched the ball loose from the ball carrier, and Dell Pettus recovered. After taking advantage of the turnover, New England quickly went three-and-out on its next drive. A 27-yard Owen punt return also put Indianapolis back into Patriots territory, but as Richardson scrambled into the red zone, veteran linebacker K.J. Britt forced another fumble. Defensive tackle Isaiah Iton’s recovery set the offense up at their own 18, where two first-down completions to receivers Cameron Dorner and Efton Chism sparked a 12-yard Kyle Williams touchdown. The second-year receiver’s quick release off the line of scrimmage separated him from the opposing defensive back to complete a 12-play, 82-yard drive. Borregales then secured the extra-point attempt. [Patriots 10 : 0 Colts] Still, the Colts sought to score before halftime. Richardson punched the ball in on a quarterback sneak as the offense went 69 yards for the score. Two Will Mallory catches totaling 37 yards set Indianapolis up in the red zone. Canada tipped the second completion, but Mallory showcased exceptional ball-tracking skills to reel it in. [Patriots 10 : 7 Colts] In one last effort before the first half expired, DeVito tried to hit Williams downfield, but the pass fell incomplete. The pair previously connected on a 25-yard pass, breaking past midfield. A Baringer punt from the Colts’ 43-yard line pinned Indianapolis at its own eight. The opposing offense reached midfield as Colts kicker Blake Grupe missed wide right from 61 yards out entering the break. Third Quarter After securing a new set of downs, New England safety John Saunders Jr. intercepted Indianapolis quarterback Riley Leonard on a deep pass intended for receiver Eli Pancol on a skinny post. Saunders added better field positioning as well, returning the takeaway into Colts territory. With rookie quarterback Behren Morton now taking over as the signal caller for the Patriots, the offense found itself in a 3rd-and-two situation following two Jam Miller rushes, but Lan Larison couldn’t convert. New England subsequently opted to kick with Borregales, who drilled the 52-yard attempt on a low snap. [Patriots 13 : 7 Colts] Borregales then had a chance to add another field goal to his game resume after an Indianapolis three-and-out. Despite the opportunity, however, the kick sailed wide left of the uprights. And as a result, the Colts took over at their own 45-yard line. An 18-yard Anderson Castle rush broke their offense into the red zone, but after a third-down penalty erased a conversion, Bradyn Swinson drew fourth-down pressure to force an incompletion. Fourth Quarter After the turnover on downs, starting at the six-yard line, Morton connected with Tejhaun Palmer on a 15-yard slant to create breathing room on his first drive of the fourth frame. Still, quick pressure and a sack on back-to-back plays after an injury to guard Andrew Rupchich forced New England to punt after gaining momentum. Shortly after Indianapolis regained possession at its own 21, both teams traded punts. Two incompletions for the Colts led to a three-and-out, and an offensive holding penalty that eliminated a Hassan Haskins first-down rush also forced the Patriots to punt. Halfway through the quarter, Indianapolis chipped into New England’s lead with a 46-yard field goal from kicker Spencer Shrader. The Colts were just shy of the red zone after two chunk completions to receivers Samir Hagans and Raylen Sharpe. [Patriots 13 : 10 Colts] The Patriots couldn’t respond on their following drive as two negative JaMycal Hasty rush attempts prematurely ended their drive. Nearing the end of the contest, Indianapolis found the tie with a 61-yard field goal delivered by Shrader with 1:16 on the clock. The Colts progressed 42 yards downfield from their own 15. [Patriots 13 : 13 Colts] With just over one minute remaining on the clock, Behren Morton led New England’s offense into field goal territory from the Patriots’ 27-yard line. Borregales had an opportunity to regain the lead with 10 seconds on the clock, but his kick trailed left of the goalpost. Indianapolis failed to score on a last-second heave from Leonard.

title: What placing Terrell Jennings on injured reserve means for the Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots announced a series of roster moves before their preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts. They made the signing of veteran free agent JaMycal Hasty official, an acquisition we already talked about here and analyzed here, while also placing fellow running back Terrell Jennings on injured reserve. Let’s take a step back […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 9: Terrell Jennings #26 of the New England Patriots stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on November 9, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots announced a series of roster moves before their preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts. They made the signing of veteran free agent JaMycal Hasty official, an acquisition we already talked about here and analyzed here , while also placing fellow running back Terrell Jennings on injured reserve . Let’s take a step back and analyze what the latter of the two transactions means for the club. Out for the year The NFL recently tweaked its injured reserve rules last year, allowing teams to reactivate up to two players sent to injured reserve on the final day of roster cuts. With Jennings being moved to the reserve list on August 13, however, he is not eligible for that treatment: his season is over. Assuming that recently-released Myles Montgomery clears waivers, that means Jennings will become the fifth player whose season has found its end before even the first preseason snap. Also in the same boat than the two running backs are tight end Julian Hill and wide receivers Jimmy Kibble and Jeremiah Webb. For Jennings himself, this marks a second straight season ended on injured reserve. Last year, he was moved to IR in mid-December and while later returning to practice was never actually activated and reverted back to the list before the Super Bowl. RB competition changes again As we mentioned in our position battle analysis from earlier on Thursday, Jennings’ return after opening training camp on the non-football injury list turned the running back competition on its head. He immediately slotted in the No. 3 role behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson, and did not cede any ground since. With him now out of the picture, however, the competition and the entire composition of the group have changed dramatically. For now, the running back depth chart looks like this : Running back (8): Rhamondre Stevenson (38), TreVeyon Henderson (32), Reggie Gilliam (44 | FB), Lan Larison (34), Jam Miller (30), Hassan Haskins (—), JaMycal Hasty (—) IR (2): Terrell Jennings, Myles Montgomery The aforementioned Stevenson and Henderson are locked into their roster spots, as is fullback Reggie Gilliam. Who will be the third back, meanwhile, remains to be determined after neither Lan Larison nor Jam Miller could seize the opportunities they had while Jennings was out the first time. Maybe newly-signed Hassan Haskins or JaMycal Hasty can make some noise. Both have familiarity playing under Mike Vrabel and experience in the NFL both from an offensive and a special teams perspective, which brings us to: Special teams impact While most of the focus surrounding Jennings’ move to season-ending IR will be on his role. as the third running back, his contributions in the game’s third phase cannot be underestimated either. After all, he had been part of multiple starting special teams units during training camp: he lined up as a kickoff return option during Tuesday’s joint practice alongside Kyle Williams, Efton Chism and Lan Larison, and also had been used on the punt team. As noted above, the Patriots’ replacement running backs, Hassan Haskins and JaMycal Hasty, both have special teams experience as well. Still, looking at the Jennings injury through a kicking game lens shows just how valuable of a contributor he could have been in 2026. Possible cap savings Moving Jennings to injured reserve does not change the Patriots’ salary cap number. While the transaction does remove his $1.075 million base salary from the active roster, he is still getting paid while on IR Meanwhile, the player that will be taking his spot on the Top 51 list is carrying the same salary. There is a chance that the Patriots could limit Jennings’ cap impact at one point, in case they exercise a split salary provision. Depending on the agreement, this would end up slightly decreasing his cap hit. Second shoe has dropped When we broke down the as-of-then-unofficial JaMycal Hasty signing earlier on Thursday, we mentioned that a second shoe was about to drop. Hasty would have put them over the offseason roster limit, which necessitated a follow-up move. We now know that it was placed Jennings on IR. Consequently, the Patriots head into Thursday night’s game against the Colts with 91 players on their active roster. They are able to carry 91 instead of the typical 90 because offensive tackle Lorenz Meth has a roster exemption due to his status as an international player.

title: Patriots place Terrell Jennings on injured reserve after adding two running backs
summary: In Foxborough, the hours leading up to the preseason opener brought a backfield shakeup. The New England Patriots placed running back Terrell Jennings on injured reserve Thursday, officially ending his campaign before the 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff at Gillette Stadium against the Indianapolis Colts. The move follows the midweek workouts and additions of veteran running […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - DECEMBER 2: Terrell Jennings #26 of the New England Patriots runs back a kick off during the game against the New York Giants at Gillette Stadium on December 2, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts.(Photo By Winslow Townson/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Foxborough, the hours leading up to the preseason opener brought a backfield shakeup. The New England Patriots placed running back Terrell Jennings on injured reserve Thursday, officially ending his campaign before the 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff at Gillette Stadium against the Indianapolis Colts. The move follows the midweek workouts and additions of veteran running backs Hassan Haskins and JaMycal Hasty . And it shifts the No. 3 spot on the depth chart behind incumbents Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson, with sophomore Lan Larison and seventh-round draft pick Jam Miller also battling for a place on the 53-man roster. That was where a former undrafted arrival out of Florida A&M had spent parts of the past two regular seasons. Jennings, 25, originally signed with the Patriots after attending rookie minicamp on a tryout basis back in 2024. The 6-foot, 222-pounder has since made 10 appearances for the organization. He rose from the practice squad to the active roster over the course of his rookie year. And in 2025, after reaching the league limit in standard elevations, he returned to the 53. Rushing for his first NFL touchdown last fall, Jennings stands with 115 scrimmage yards through 37 touches as a Patriot. Also having a hand in three tackles and two kickoff returns, his career has spanned 79 snaps on offense and 69 snaps on special teams. He had finished the team’s run to Super Bowl LX on injured reserve after his 21-day practice window expired in February. In additional backfield movement, rookie rusher Myles Montgomery reverted to New England’s injured reserve on Thursday, according to the league’s transaction wire. Montgomery, 23, had been waived with an injury designation the afternoon prior and went unclaimed. The 5-foot-10, 205-pound back agreed to terms as part of the club’s undrafted class in May. Spending three years at Cincinnati before transferring to Central Florida for his final two years of eligibility, the former Knights captain appeared in 41 collegiate games. title: Saints rookie report – Preseason Week 1
summary: Welcome to this season’s first edition of the New Orleans Saints rookie report. This year’s class should be as exciting as what we saw in 2025, so let’s not waste time for the Week 1 preseason preview. WR Jordyn Tyson Although the Saints may be smart to not risk Jordyn Tyson’s health in preseason, I […]
full_text: Welcome to this season’s first edition of the New Orleans Saints rookie report. This year’s class should be as exciting as what we saw in 2025, so let’s not waste time for the Week 1 preseason preview. WR Jordyn Tyson Although the Saints may be smart to not risk Jordyn Tyson’s health in preseason, I would not be surprised if he gets some game time before the regular season. He’s still a rookie, and getting reps on an NFL field will prepare him for the season. Tyson is one of the Saints’ best offensive players right away, and fans should be excited to see him play, but it might not happen right away. DT Christen Miller The opposite of Tyson’s situation, Christen Miller should have plenty of playing time. The second-round pick has been dealing with some minor injuries this offseason, but he is back in practice and should be ready for Saturday. With other injuries hitting the defensive tackle room, Miller is likely going to be the starting nose tackle for the preseason. Even if Davon Godchaux was healthy, Miller starting for now was likely, and he has a really good opportunity to show the coaching staff that he can play right away during the regular season. TE Oscar Delp Juwan Johnson is likely not going to play much in preseason, which means it’s Oscar Delp’s time to shine. The rookie’s production in college was subpar, but the talent was always there. His athletic ability sets him apart from other TEs, and his blocking will really help the team. During the regular season, his snaps are expected to be lower during his rookie season, so the preseason could be the place we see him have the most impact. It’s going to be very interesting to see his utilization in the red zone as well. G Jeremiah Wright Another player who has had some minor injuries in training camp, Jeremiah Wright is our first depth piece from the draft class who may not see the field this season. Preseason is going to be extremely important for the rookie, and if he is able to have a good few games, competing for the starting spot may not be out of the question. But that’s unlikely, since Wright is more of a developmental prospect, even if he’s had a good start to camp. WRs Bryce Lance and Barion Brown With both of the next rookies being WRs and having very similar camps so far, I wanted to put them together. Bryce Lance has been super consistent in training camp, and adding a sprinkle of big plays, he has been a standout player. Barion Brown has been a big-play machine, and while he has had some drops, he has been mostly consistent overall. These two are not going to break that top 3 WR group that the Saints have, but they can be heavy contributors right away, and preseason is going to be a great way to show that. DBs Lorenzo Styles Jr. and TJ Hall Similar to Lance and Brown, Lorenzo Styles Jr. and TJ Hall can also be grouped together. Both are DBs that will impact special teams right away, but not really defense. Each will be able to show in preseason what they could potentially bring to the defense now and possibly in the future, but again, that’s unlikely in their rookie seasons. Styles Jr. is extremely athletic and has some defensive versatility that allows him to step in at safety and CB, while Hall can play outside corner or slot. With injuries, these two may have some starting playtime this season, but their snaps on defense will mostly come in preseason.

summary: The unfortunate part about the NFL news cycle at this stage of the calendar is that injuries tend to make up a lion’s share of the headlines. That’s been true in New Orleans, where, among the injuries picked up so far in training camp, came the news of Dillon Radunz’s ACL tear, which will sideline […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - FEBRUARY 28: Auburn offensive lineman Jeremiah Wright answers questions from the media during the NFL Scouting Combine on February 28, 2026 at the Indiana Convention Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The unfortunate part about the NFL news cycle at this stage of the calendar is that injuries tend to make up a lion’s share of the headlines. That’s been true in New Orleans, where, among the injuries picked up so far in training camp, came the news of Dillon Radunz’s ACL tear, which will sideline him until 2027. The versatile offensive lineman was set to play a key role as a depth piece across the line this year. In his absence, a key name to look out for is Saints rookie and fourth-round draft pick out of Auburn, Jeremiah Wright. Head coach Kellen Moore was asked about Wright after Tuesday’s session. “Good player, physical player,” said Moore. “These will be great opportunities for him in these preseason games, a ton of reps, but also these joint practices to see some other competition, so it’ll be great for him.” “I love what he’s doing right now, and he’s playing some really good football.” With a month still to go before the regular season, it remains to be seen whether Wright will be deemed ready to play a role from week one. But Radunz’s injury emphasizes the need for depth pieces to step up along the O-Line. Wright starred at right guard over the last two seasons at Auburn. He’s a name to keep a close eye on as preseason unfolds. How else might the Saints replace Radunz’s impact? Let us know below!

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about after Day 14 of Giants training camp. Who is the Giants’ top performer so far at camp? | ESPN.com TE Isaiah Likely. The offseason acquisition has been the Giants’ No. 1 receiver with Malik Nabers not participating in team drills. He’s been quarterback Jaxson Dart’s safety net, leading all first-team receivers in catches by a wide margin. “Zay’s done a great job,” offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said. The way Likely smoothly gets in and out of breaks has just looked different from incumbent starter Theo Johnson. He also seems to have the best handle on the new offense given his familiarity with coach John Harbaugh and senior offensive assistant Greg Roman from Baltimore. Given the way Dart likes to throw to his tight ends, it suggests that Likely is in for a breakout season given the chemistry they already have developed. Harbaugh on preseason playing time "I value first-team reps very much. You have to measure that against the risk. There is risk, as well." John Harbaugh talks about the risk and reward of playing the Giants' starters in the preseason: pic.twitter.com/azk1sfEVOz — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) August 13, 2026 The somewhat awkward position battle unfolding at Giants camp | New York Post Jason Pinnock hasn’t reacquired his old No. 27 jersey number from his former protégé Tyler Nubin, but he has begun to steal away some starting safety snaps. Pinnock and Nubin are close enough friends that they are invited to each other’s baby showers — and Nubin to Pinnock’s upcoming wedding — but that doesn’t mean the battle for playing time is not intense. Quite the opposite, actually. The Giants listed Nubin and Holland as starters and Pinnock and Washington as backups on their first unofficial depth chart. Holland’s place is secure, while Nubin has gone from the beneficiary of early quiet praise from Harbaugh to rocky footing. “That’s my brother,” Pinnock said, “[but] this is what comes with the sport. We’re on each other. We’re probably each other’s biggest competitor, and we’re on each other’s ass. It just is what it is.” Do Giants need reinforcements at RB, or can Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr. carry the load? | The Athletic Last year, the Giants finished 18th in yards per carry (4.3), 25th in rushing success rate and 16th in explosive run rate. However, some of the heavy lifting in those numbers was done by quarterback Jaxson Dart, who rushed for 487 yards and nine scores last season. When you remove QB runs, the Giants fell to 25th in yards per carry (4.0), 27th in rushing success rate and 20th in explosive run rate. Those numbers beg the question: Do the Giants have the necessary components to be as effective on the ground as they want to be? From idol to teammate: New York Giants players in awe of Odell Beckham Jr. | USAToday.com “I think as a player, he’s still the same caliber player, but I’ve never been around him in a building,” said Winston. “I only knew him as this football icon, the guy that made one-handed catches, and if you put the ball in his hand, he was going to make a play. “But to see him being the teammate that he is — it’s very funny seeing he and Malachi (Fields). Because Malachi — most of the young guys — they’re Odell Beckham Jr. fans. It’s true. Jalin Hyatt got 13 because he’s an Odell Beckham Jr. fan. So, it’s fun to see him putting the past in the past and focusing on getting better every day.” Giants’ John Harbaugh pushes back on ‘way overblown’ narrative | NJ.com So what does Harbaugh think of the notion that he could wear down the Giants by conducting this sort of camp? “I feel like it’s just football practice,” he said, adding that he wants players who love football. “So these practices out here, I think it’s way overblown about how hard they are. They’re good, crisp, sharp, efficient practices. We’re chasing the fundamentals. We’re trying to understand situations. We’re trying to build our systems out, so we can execute under pressure and be our best. That’s what we’re working toward.” Mike Lupica: It’s no regular preseason game for John Harbaugh, Giants | New York Daily News Whatever the Giants are going to be — and whether or not they can be what they once were — all begins on Saturday afternoon against the Vikings. Preseason game or not. This is where the John Harbaugh Era begins, with the new coach under more pressure on his way through the door as any Giants coach has ever faced. Whether or not Dart is on the field Saturday, Giants fans will let Harbaugh know — long and loud — just how happy they are that he is on that field…Then Harbaugh hit the open market. The Giants needed someone exactly like him so much they probably would have thrown in naming rights to the big, ugly gray bowl if he’d asked for that. And from the day he was hired, he really has been swept along by the sound of applause. Giants fans don’t just want Harbaugh on that wall. They need him on that wall. Sometimes even the first preseason game feels as if it matters. It’s because of how much Giants fans want their team to matter again. title: Fantasy Football 2026: Sleepers!
summary: At long last, draft season for season-long redraft fantasy leagues is right around the corner. Are you ready? Home Leagues that use a redraft format are still the backbone of the fantasy football world, and from the middle of August through Labor Day weekend, countless home, work, and family leagues will go through the annual […]
full_text: Can Shahid tilt the field in Seattle? | Getty Images At long last, draft season for season-long redraft fantasy leagues is right around the corner. Are you ready? Home Leagues that use a redraft format are still the backbone of the fantasy football world, and from the middle of August through Labor Day weekend, countless home, work, and family leagues will go through the annual ritual of player selection. Family ties, work relationships, and friendships will be strengthened — or maybe tested — through a shared passion and friendly competition. Bragging rights are on the line. Prize money is on the line. Last place punishments loom. It really is the best. Crushing your draft in a “home” league is very satisfying. But to do that you can’t just nail picking your starting lineup early in the process. Selections made towards the back end of the proceedings can make a huge difference, and I don’t mean grabbing your DST and kicker with your last two picks. Today I’m giving you a handful of sleepers to target in the double-digit rounds. What’s a sleeper? Definitions vary, but for me it’s a player who’s likely to be available late in drafts (or who might not get drafted at all), and who brings an upside opportunity that could translate into a meaningful contribution in fantasy this year. Players like Kyler Murray, Jonathon Brooks, Blake Corum, Josh Downs, Jordyn Tyson, Isaiah Likely, and Mark Andrews will all go in the first 120 picks or so of most drafts and don’t qualify as “sleepers” this year. We’re going deeper than that, folks. For this exercise, I’m only going to list quarterbacks, running backs, wide receivers, and tight ends whose current Expert Consensus Ranking (ECR) is outside the Top-132. These are players who will often be available to you after completion of the 11 th round in 12-team leagues, or who you can nab for a dollar or two in your auction draft. You’ll want to have sleeper targets ready when the draft hits the point where your league mates start to lose focus, are five or six beers in, and are on their phones bragging about their stacked team. ECRs shown are for Half-point PPR, and any player rankings shown are also Half PPR, on a fantasy points per game (FPPG) basis, with Week 18 excluded. Most sleeper calls won’t hit. That’s kind of the point. The majority of late-round picks will end up just riding your bench or being dropped. When you take swings with minimal draft capital, you get what you pay for. But if you totally whiff on your late picks, you’ll be at a disadvantage vs. managers who found value at the end of the draft. You usually need to hit on a sleeper or two to win your league. Here’s a link to all of my preseason fantasy football content here at Big Blue View, including my July rankings, position previews, random thoughts, and more: Fantasy Football Hub . Coming soon: A Giants fantasy preview, and players to target and avoid at average draft cost. Here we go, as they say in Pittsburgh. Listed below are some cheaply priced players who bring the kind of upside you want with your late-round dart throws. Quarterback Cutoff: B. Mayfield (ECR 120, QB18), J. Love (ECR 122, QB19), T. Shough (ECR 125 (QB20). Sleepers: Malik Willis (ECR 134, QB21) Sam Darnold (ECR 141, QB23) Cam Ward (ECR 153, QB24) Jacoby Brissett (ECR: 173, QB27) Quarterback is as deep as it’s ever been. Just look at the names right above the cutoff line and where they’re ranked. There are 17 QBs ranked ahead of that trio. Wow. Most of the players I listed as sleepers won’t get drafted in 1-QB leagues, but almost all will be taken in Superflex leagues where it’s good to get three viable options if you can. Last year I had Matt Stafford and Jaxson Dart listed here. While I don’t think any of the sleepers listed above will hit like those two did (QB5 and QB12, respectively), there’s upside here, if you want to wait on your second quarterback in a Superflex or feel like throwing a dart on a second QB (in a 1-QB league) with a very late pick. Willis only has a handful of starts to his name, but his per-start rushing average is around 60 yards per game, which is more than all-time NFL leader Lamar Jackson’s 56. His rushing upside is tantalizing. The Dolphins have a receiver room full of unknowns and rookies, but they should be playing from behind regularly and it’s unlikely Willis gets benched unless he’s truly awful, given what they paid him and what else they have. He’s worth a swing. Ward’s rookie season was uneven to say the least, but he should benefit from the arrival of new OC Brian Daboll and the additions of Carnell Tate and Wan’Dale Robinson. Darnold might need to air it out more with Kenneth Walker gone and Zach Charbonnet on the mend, and he has the highest floor of the quarterbacks listed. Brissett will probably give way to Carson Beck at some point, but the Cardinals might be even worse than Miami and we saw what Brissett did last season while losing game after game (QB4 from Weeks 6-15), and he’s got weaponry. I do think Arizona’s new regime will try to be a little more balanced on offense, but still, Brissett has QB1 upside. Running Back Cutoff: T. Tracy, Jr. (ECR 126, RB42), C. Rodriguez, Jr. (ECR 127, RB43). Sleepers: Tank Bigsby (ECR 148, RB50) Keaton Mitchell (ECR 149, RB51) Jonah Coleman (R) (ECR 157, RB54) Marshawn Lloyd (ECR 184, RB61) I’m a big believer in grabbing several backup running backs with some of my later picks. You just never know when an injury will open the door to a big opportunity, and those can be league-winner situations. Waiver wire stampedes for backup running backs who get thrust into a starting role are a common occurrence in fantasy. Why not take a few preemptive swings to see if you can jump the line on that? Maybe you get a roster clogger, but it’s worth the potential upside if you can keep the space on your bench. The guys I’ve listed above are my favorite targets among the RBs going after Round 11. Out of all the handcuffs/backups to Top-12 RBs in this range of the draft, I think Bigsby has the best odds of stepping into a very high percentage of the starter’s role in the event of injury, and Saquon Barkley is 29. On top of that, his 728 touches over the last two seasons (including playoffs) are the most in the NFL. Mike McDaniel knows how to get the most out of a speed back, and Mitchell should have a nice change-of-pace and passing down role on the Chargers. Lloyd could see a big opportunity if Josh Jacobs gets hurt again or faces league discipline, which is still a possibility. Coleman is an intriguing rookie – he’s big and strong which could earn him some goal-line reps, and he’s good in the passing game, which is a big plus for a back on a Sean Payton team. I won’t be shocked if he ends up being the top back (for fantasy) in Denver by the second half of the season. Deep Sleepers (ECR of 190 or lower) : Jaydon Blue, Nick Singleton (R), Kaytron Allen (R), Kaelon Black (R) Wide Receiver: Cutoff: J. Coker , K. Shakir , S. Diggs , R. Doubs (ECR 128-131, WR50-53). Sleepers: Matthew Golden (ECR 136, WR55) Rashid Shaheed (ECR 138, WR56) Denzel Boston (ECR 161, WR60) D’Zhuan Stribling (R) (ECR 168, WR64) Tre Harris (ECR 176, WR67) Ryan Flournoy (ECR 183, WR69) Jalen Nailor (ECR 188, WR70) Wide receiver is a good place to shop in Rounds 8-11, and there are several high upside guys who I plan to target in that range ( Jordyn Tyson, Chris Godwin, Josh Downs, and Jayden Reed head the list). It’s a decent part of the draft for WR value. It thins out some after that, and again, I plan on hammering backup running backs in the later rounds. It’s also easier to find serviceable wide receivers on the waiver wire as compared to RBs, which further argues for filling out your bench late with a bias towards RBs over WRs. Still, receiver is a deep position, and there are some sleepers with nice upside that you can find in the later rounds as well. Golden was disappointing as a first-round pick rookie, but with the WR room in Green Bay…

title: NY Giants’ young placekickers have been impressive this summer
summary: When New York Giants special teams coordinator Chris Horton met the media earlier this week, the first question he got was about the team’s placekicking competition. Horton laughed and said, “You want to start at the kicker battle?” Of course. Where else was there to start except the placekicking competition between Dominic Zvada and Ben […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants kicker Ben Sauls in a game | Getty Images When New York Giants special teams coordinator Chris Horton met the media earlier this week, the first question he got was about the team’s placekicking competition. Horton laughed and said, “You want to start at the kicker battle?” Of course. Where else was there to start except the placekicking competition between Dominic Zvada and Ben Sauls ? The position has been a problem for the Giants for several years. Injuries and poor decisions in the kicking game cost the Giants games, and the team finally moved on from Graham Gano this offseason. The Giants attempted to replace Gano with a three-way kicking competition between Sauls, Zvada, and veteran kicker Jason Sanders. It was a surprise when the Giants released Sanders earlier in the offseason. That move left them with three-game veteran Sauls and Zvada, an undrafted rookie. Sauls was seen as an early favorite, as he had in-game experience with the Giants in 2025, while Zvada was coming off a rough year at Michigan. However, Sauls struggled early in the offseason while Zvada seemingly reverted to his All-American form from 2024. “It’s two young guys that are doing very well,” Horton said. “Both guys’ leg talent is there. Both guys, where they are right now from where they were during this spring, I mean, it’s been tremendous growth just watching these guys go out and compete against each other. They know that they’re in a competition, and they come out every day, and they work hard. “It’s just like any other position, just like any other thing. We all got to start somewhere, right? Somebody’s just got to be willing to give you an opportunity, but that opportunity, like I said, comes with the process, and once you go through the process, and you follow that process, and you believe in yourself, everything else takes care of itself because it comes with discipline and consistency, right?” Zvada is coming off of a rough 2025 season at Michigan. Horton says that Zvada’s process has been isolating the factors that led to him being inconsistent and working on those issues. So far, the results have been outstanding. “You watch him [Zvada], you watch his form, you watch him at the Combine, and you just ask him what do you think led to those missed kicks?” Horton said. “And it was a lot of things; he talked about it being a lot of things, and then we just tried to find a ball. We tried to find an operation that fit him, and we changed a couple things, and then he’s kicking the ball straight.” Zvada is indeed kicking straight through the uprights, going 7-for-7 in Wednesday’s practice. He also showed off his leg and was good from 50, 53, and 62 yards. One aspect of special teams that often goes unnoticed is how delicate the whole operation can be. If the timing is off by a fraction of a second, or the angle of the hold is off by a degree, it can result in a bad miss 60 yards down the field. And in that vein, Horton noted that it’s difficult for a holder to switch sides between a left- and right-footed kicker. Horton added that part of Sauls’ kicking issues earlier in the offseason may be related to how Stout was holding the ball. “So, they [Sauls’ kicks] would all tail off to the right,” Horton said. “It was a combination of how you hold the ball, the movement on the ball, where Jordan (Stout) should seat the ball, the kind of lean and all those things, so the ball matches up to the foot a little bit better.” Horton credited both Sauls and Stout for the work they did in the stretch between minicamp and training camp to polish that part of the operation. “Since he [Sauls] left this spring, he left, he came back, and he’s just hitting balls, straight balls, straight balls, and that’s what we want to see, right? I mean, the guy kicked well last year. He was 8 for 8, so he kicked well.” And this is what’s making the kicking competition so interesting: The Giants seem to have two good young kickers on their hands. Sauls only missed one kick in Wednesday’s practice (a 45-yard attempt), making 5 of 6 kicks and was also good from 50 and 53 yards. Ultimately, the Giants find themselves in an uncommon position for NFL teams. Teams generally struggle to trust young specialists, as they’re often in high-leverage situations and the game may depend on them to execute the first time, every time. Horton believes that trust isn’t necessarily a function of age or experience, so much as built through time and work. The Giants are giving all three of their young specialists — Sauls, Zvada, and long snapper Ben Mann — golden opportunities to earn trust this summer. “Trust comes with a lot of responsibility, and I think it’s easy,” Horton said. “It’s not because they’re young you have to find a way to trust them. It’s what they do when they’re out there. You build trust through your work. You build trust through your preparation, and the preparation that both these guys are bringing every day. We’re going to have to trust them in the big moments, and we try to put them in those situations so when they go out there, we feel pretty good about it.”

summary: The New York Giants will practice Thursday afternoon at Quest Diagnostics Training Center, their 14th practice of training camp. Head coach John Harbaugh said Wednesday that he can see players beginning to think about having a game […]
full_text: The New York Giants will practice Thursday afternoon at Quest Diagnostics Training Center, their 14th practice of training camp. It will be the final workout prior to Saturday’s preseason opener at MetLife Stadium against the Minnesota Vikings. Head coach John Harbaugh said Wednesday that he can see players beginning to think about having a game to play this weekend. “Guys can feel it,” Harbaugh said. “It’s always the last couple days here. You get that grind 10, 12 days in and now you’ve got the three, four days, we’re still trying to get better. We’re still trying to focus on technique. We’re making the most of these days and I’m preaching that, but you can see their attention is starting to go toward the game.” A few things to note regarding Thursday’s practice: Is it possible Terrion Arnold could be part of it? Harbaugh certainly does not seem to be against the idea of signing Arnold , despite his serious legal situation. Will any of the Giants’ long list of injured players get back on the field? This practice will not be in pads. How hard will they go? Harbaugh admitted backing down a bit in terms of the intensity of practice on Wednesday. Please come back after practice for all of the news, highlights, and analysis.

Here are the stories you need to know about after Day 13 of Giants training camp. 2026 NFC East preview, offseason recap for Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders & Giants | The Athletic Headline: John Harbaugh hired. “He pulls the best out of everybody,” said second-year edge rusher Abdul Carter, in Michael Silver’s story about how the new coach gives New York direction. After posting just three losing records in 18 seasons with the Ravens, is Harbaugh’s winning pedigree enough to fix the Giants? Projection: 6-11. It’s easy to get excited about these Giants. They have a young core, a well-pedigreed coach and a quarterback who nearly began his career 3-1 (if not for that 33-point fourth-quarter collapse). But Harbaugh’s Ravens struggled with injuries and maintaining leads. His new team has the same problems. I’ll take the under in Year 1.\ Predicting Every NFL Division’s Standings for 2026 Season Ahead of Preseason Week 1 | Bleacher Report New York Giants: 7-10. Thus far, the Giants’ offense has struggled at training camp. Given offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s mediocre play-calling resume, it all makes sense. In three out of four years as the Chicago Bears’ primary play-caller, his offenses ranked 22nd or worse in scoring and 24th or worse in total yards. He has a dynamic quarterback in Jaxson Dart, but the young signal-caller must learn to protect himself in a run-first offense. Wideout Malik Nabers may need time to get back to 100 percent coming off a torn ACL. The Giants have too many offensive question marks to feel good about their season outlook. 2026 NFL Preseason Week 1: 10 things to watch | NFL.com 8) New bullies on the block? After months of talk about John Harbaugh building a new culture with the Giants, will all the chatter translate to the field? For a team with one winning season in the last nine campaigns, there certainly seems to be a newfound confidence. Harbaugh favorite Patrick Ricard, the fullback who followed the Super Bowl-winning coach from Baltimore to Big Blue this offseason, told NFL Network this week that the Giants want to “bully” any team that comes into MetLife Stadium. That would be a major departure from the G-Men we’ve come to know over the past decade, and first up in 2026 are the Vikings on Saturday. Remember, the Ravens didn’t do enough bullying in the final season of Harbaugh’s 18-year tenure with the team, which is why he was available this offseason. Will a fresh start lead to different results right away? 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three | PFF 23. New York Giants. Andrew Thomas was arguably the Giants’ best player last year, earning a 90.3 PFF grade that tied his career high. His issue has been staying healthy, having missed significant time in both 2023 and 2024. They drafted Francis Mauigoa in the first round, and if he can hit the ground running, then the unit looks a lot stronger, but it’s a group that just might be another season away from making a bigger impact.
